lines.text: ## 1. Asking once more, aware of the anger (ON) — Gen 18:30, 18:32; Judg 6:39

answer.not_an_observation: heading
answer.reason: the heading of a phenomenon, with the verses it covers

lines.text: - Abraham: "Oh let not the Lord be angry, and I will speak. Suppose thirty are found there" (Gen 18:30), and at the last: "Oh let not the Lord be angry, and I will speak again but this once. Suppose ten" (18:32).
- Gideon, after the fleece was wet: "Let not your anger burn against me; let me speak just once more. Please let me test just once more with the fleece" (Judg 6:39).

- **Where it comes from.** From **knowing the distance** and asking anyway. Abraham says twice, "I have undertaken to speak to the Lord, I who am but dust and ashes" (Gen 18:27; 18:31). Gideon has already had his sign (Judg 6:38). **The asker knows that the request presses on God's patience.**
- **Every request is granted, and no anger comes.** "I will not do it, if I find thirty there" (Gen 18:30); "God did so that night" (Judg 6:40). **The anger feared never appears in either passage.**
- **What it leads to.** The asker stops. Abraham stops at ten and "returned to his place" (Gen 18:33). **The asker, not God, sets the limit** ("but this once").

- **Seat.** None in-verse or in ±3. The self-description "dust and ashes" (Gen 18:27) does the seat's work: **the asker places himself before God as creature**. Job repents "in dust and ashes" (Job 42:6), read in §25 of this document. **Pointer only:** the phrase links the bold asker and the humbled sufferer.
## 2. God's anger at Moses (MS, B6) — Exo 4:14; Deu 1:37; 3:26; 4:21 · (v2) Psa 106:32

answer.not_an_observation: heading
answer.reason: the heading of a phenomenon, with the verses it covers

lines.text: - **At the call:** "Oh, my Lord, please send someone else." "Then the anger of the Lord was kindled against Moses" (Exo 4:13–14). **The anger is answered at once by provision:** Aaron "is coming out to meet you, and when he sees you, he will be glad in his heart" (4:14); "I will be with your mouth and with his mouth" (4:15).

- **At the end:** "Even with me the Lord was angry on your account and said, 'You also shall not go in there'" (Deu 1:37); "the Lord was angry with me because of you and would not listen to me … 'Enough from you; do not speak to me of this matter again'" (3:26); "I must die in this land; I must not go over the Jordan" (4:21–22).

- Deuteronomy: **"on your account" / "because of you"**, three times (Deu 1:37; 3:26; 4:21). Moses traces the anger at himself to the people. (The narrative cause, Meribah, is U1 §12.) **The leader bears God's anger as the people's leader, and says so.**

- **The plea refused, and something else given instead.** Moses "pleaded with the Lord" (Deu 3:23–25). The answer was "Enough", then "lift up your eyes … and look at it with your eyes" (3:27). **The land is given to the eye, not the foot.**

- **The anger is followed each time by a charge to hand on:** "Encourage him" (Deu 1:38); "charge Joshua, and encourage and strengthen him" (3:28). In Exo 4 a partner is given, and in Deuteronomy a successor. **The anger does not end the man's service. It reshapes it.**

- **What it leads to.** Moses **speaks of his exclusion to the people as a warning to them**. Deu 4:21–22 is followed at once by "Take care, lest you forget the covenant" (4:23) and "the Lord your God is a consuming fire" (4:24). **His own bearing of the anger becomes his teaching.**

- **In the verse:** Exo 4:14 "glad in his heart". **The other party's (Aaron's). Genuine.** Already read in G v3 §13.2 ("the heart goes out to meet"). **Read from the M02 side, it shows that the anger at Moses is met with a glad heart coming towards him.**
- **Outside the verse:** none in Deu 1:34–40; 3:23–29; 4:18–25.

- **(v2) Part B: Psa 106:32.** "They angered him at the waters of Meribah, and it went ill with Moses on their account, for they made his spirit bitter, and he spoke rashly with his lips" (Psa 106:32–33).

- **Whose spirit is not determinable.** The M47 spirit classification v2 marks Psa 106:33 as [U] (#1880 item C-R4; C v3 R4). It could be Moses' spirit embittered, or God's Spirit rebelled against (compare Isa 63:10). **Either way, the verse ties Meribah to Moses' loss "on their account".**

answer.not_an_observation: heading
answer.reason: the heading of a phenomenon, with the verses it covers

lines.text: - **Sung by the rescued:** "you send out your fury; it consumes them like stubble" (Exo 15:7).
- **Promised to the obedient:** "if you carefully obey his voice … then I will be an enemy to your enemies and an adversary to your adversaries" (Exo 23:22).
- **Released by the cry of the weak:** "If you do mistreat them, and they cry out to me, I will surely hear their cry, and my wrath will burn" (Exo 22:23–24).
- **Released by the psalmist's call:** "In my distress I called upon the Lord … my cry came to his ears. Then the earth reeled … because he was angry" (2Sa 22:7–8).

- **Where it comes from.** From **the human cry**: the widow's and orphan's (Exo 22:23), the poor debtor's (22:27: "if he cries to me, I will hear, for I am compassionate"), David's "in my distress" (2Sa 22:7). **In two of the four verses, the human cry is what precedes the anger.**

- **The enemy's own appetite.** In the song, the enemy boasts, "my desire [*nephesh*] shall have its fill of them" (Exo 15:9), and is answered by the wind of God (15:10). **The enemy's appetite and God's fury meet over the same people.** Already read in F v4 §8.4 ("the enemy's soul and the pursued soul").

- **The same anger threatens the one it protects, if roles reverse.** Exo 22:24 is said to Israel about **their own** widows: "I will kill you with the sword, and your wives shall become widows". **God's anger is for the weak, whoever the oppressor is.**
- **What it leads to.** Praise (Exo 15), or deliverance (2Sa 22:17 onward, not read here).
- **Seat.** None in-verse. **Outside:** Exo 15:9 *nephesh* (the enemy's, appetite-sense) and 15:8, 10 "blast", "wind", "heart of the sea" (not inner-being). F v4 §8.4 covers 15:9. **Nothing new.**
- Psa 18:7 is the psalm text of 2Sa 22:8: "In my distress I called upon the Lord … because he was angry" (Psa 18:6–7).

- **The upright in heart, and the call to repent.** "God is a righteous judge, and a God who feels indignation every day" (Psa 7:11). This follows "you who test the minds and hearts … who saves the upright in heart" (7:9–10), and is followed by "If a man does not repent, God will whet his sword" (7:12). **The protection is for the upright in heart, and the indignation waits on repentance.**
- **The king who trusts:** "the king trusts in the Lord … Your hand will find out all your enemies" (Psa 21:7–9). The king at God's right hand: "Your people will offer themselves freely" (110:3, 5).
- **The Exodus retold:** "He made a path for his anger; he did not spare them from death" (Psa 78:50). "Then he led out his people like sheep" (78:52).
- "You shall have a song … and gladness of heart" (Isa 30:29), while "the Assyrians will be terror-stricken" (30:31).
- "As one whom his mother comforts, so I will comfort you … You shall see, and your heart shall rejoice; your bones shall flourish like the grass" (66:13–14).
- **The protected are the people the anger struck earlier:** "the Lord binds up the brokenness of his people, and heals the wounds inflicted by his blow" (Isa 30:26).
- **In the verse:** Isa 66:14 "your heart shall rejoice". **The comforted people's own. Genuine** (A v3 §4.3). Psa 78:50 "them" (*nephesh*) is the Egyptians' life. **Life-sense** (C v3 §0).
- **Outside:** Psa 7:9–10 "hearts" / "upright in heart" (D v2 §1.1, §11; E v2 §8.1, §11.3). Isa 30:29 "gladness of heart" (D v2 §7.4).
- **What part B adds.** Part A had only praise (Exo 15). **Part B places the joy of the protected in the heart.**

- **Anger for the reproached:** "Behold, I have spoken in my jealous wrath, because you have suffered the reproach of the nations" (Eze 36:6). Edom took the land "with wholehearted joy and utter contempt" (36:5). "you will soon come home" (36:8).
- "I am jealous for Zion with great jealousy, and I am jealous for her with great wrath. … I have returned to Zion" (Zec 8:2–3). "The Lord … keeps wrath for his enemies" (Nah 1:2).
- "O Lord, I have heard the report of you, and your work, O Lord, do I fear … in wrath remember mercy" (Hab 3:2)
- "Was your wrath against the rivers …? … You went out for the salvation of your people" (3:8, 13)
- the enemy came "rejoicing as if to devour the poor in secret" (3:14)
- then: "I hear, and my body trembles; my lips quiver … rottenness enters into my bones … Yet I will quietly wait for the day of trouble to come upon people who invade us" (3:16)
- and: "Though the fig tree should not blossom … yet I will rejoice in the Lord" (3:17–18)

- **Seat (v3).** **Outside:** Eze 36:5 "wholehearted joy and utter contempt" (heart and *nephesh*). **Edom's. Genuine** (A v3 §4.4; F v4 §8.3; C v3 §1.8). Hab 3:16's "body" and "bones" carry no M47 tag in the DB, so **they are bodily trembling and not a counted seat.**

answer.reason: a note, open thread or count about the work, not a finding

lines.text: ## 4. Intercession: standing before the anger for others (IN) — Exo 32:10, 32:11, 32:12; Num 16:22; Deu 9:18, 9:19, 9:20 · (v2) Psa 106:23 · (v3) Eze 9:8; Dan 9:16; Zec 1:12

answer.not_an_observation: heading
answer.reason: the heading of a phenomenon, with the verses it covers

lines.text: - **God himself leaves the door open:** "Now therefore let me alone, that my wrath may burn hot against them" (Exo 32:10). **The anger waits on whether Moses will let God alone.**

- Moses argues. He argues from **ownership**: "why does your wrath burn hot against your people, whom you have brought out" (32:11). He argues from **God's reputation**: "Why should the Egyptians say, 'With evil intent did he bring them out'?" (32:12). He argues from **promise**: "Remember Abraham, Isaac, and Israel" (32:13).
- He argues from **justice between the one and the many**: "O God, the God of the spirits of all flesh, shall one man sin, and will you be angry with all the congregation?" (Num 16:22).
- **With the body:** "I lay prostrate before the Lord … forty days and forty nights. I neither ate bread nor drank water" (Deu 9:18).
- **For the particular man:** "the Lord was so angry with Aaron that he was ready to destroy him. And I prayed for Aaron also" (Deu 9:20).

- **Where it comes from.** From **fear**. "For I was afraid of the anger and hot displeasure that the Lord bore against you" (Deu 9:19). **The intercessor's own fear of God's anger drives the plea for others.** It does not stop it.

- **Intercession sits alongside the intercessor's own anger.** The same chapter has Moses' own anger breaking the tablets (Exo 32:19; U1 §11 LD; Deu 9:17). **Moses is angry at the people and pleads for them against God's anger, within one episode.**
- **It is answered:** "the Lord relented" (Exo 32:14); "the Lord listened to me that time also" (Deu 9:19).

- **What it leads to.** The people are spared. In Deuteronomy, the memory of the intercession **is itself turned into instruction** (Deu 9:25–29, "So I lay prostrate …"), set against the people's claim to righteousness (§8).

- **In the verse:** Num 16:22 "spirits of all flesh". **God's relation to every human spirit, given as the ground of the plea. Genuine** (D v2 §3.4: "God's relation to every spirit is the ground of the plea against collective punishment"). **Nothing new.**
- **Outside:** none in Exo 32:7–15; Deu 9:15–22.
- **Pointer:** the fasting body (Deu 9:18) **does the seat's work** here, as the face and bed do in U1 §1.
- **(v2) Part B: Psa 106:23.** "Therefore he said he would destroy them — had not Moses, his chosen one, stood in the breach before him, to turn away his wrath from destroying them."
- **The psalm names Moses' intercession (Exo 32; Deu 9) "standing in the breach".** Its context is "They forgot God, their Savior" (106:21).
- forbidden: "As for you, do not pray for this people … do not intercede with me, for I will not hear you" (Jer 7:16, context of §7)
- absent: "there was no one to intercede" (Isa 59:16; §41)
- repaid with evil: Jer 18:20 (§45)

- **The prophet refused.** "while they were striking, and I was left alone, I fell upon my face, and cried, 'Ah, Lord God! Will you destroy all the remnant of Israel …?'" (Eze 9:8). **The answer is no:** "The guilt … is exceedingly great … For they say, 'The Lord has forsaken the land, and the Lord does not see.' As for me, my eye will not spare" (9:9–10). Some are spared: the mark is put "on the foreheads of the men who sigh and groan over all the abominations" (9:4, context read). **Those who grieve over the sin are marked. The one who pleads for the rest is not answered.**

- "O Lord, according to all your righteous acts, let your anger and your wrath turn away from your city Jerusalem … because for our sins, and for the iniquities of our fathers, Jerusalem … [has] become a byword" (Dan 9:16)
- "the Lord our God is righteous in all the works that he has done" (9:14)
- "for your own sake" (9:17)
- "we do not present our pleas before you because of our righteousness, but because of your great mercy" (9:18)

- **An angel intercedes:** "O Lord of hosts, how long will you have no mercy on Jerusalem …, against which you have been angry these seventy years?" This is answered with "gracious and comforting words" (Zec 1:12–13).
## 5. "Slow to anger": the name proclaimed, pleaded back, recited (SA) — Exo 34:6; Num 14:18; Neh 9:17 · (v2) Psa 86:15; 103:8; 145:8 · (v3) Mic 7:18; Nah 1:3

answer.not_an_observation: heading
answer.reason: the heading of a phenomenon, with the verses it covers

lines.text: 1. **Proclaimed and received:** "The Lord, the Lord, a God merciful and gracious, slow to anger" (Exo 34:6). Moses "quickly bowed his head toward the earth and worshiped" (34:8).

2. **Pleaded back:** Moses quotes it to God word for word as his argument: "'The Lord is slow to anger and abounding in steadfast love …' Please pardon the iniquity of this people" (Num 14:18–19). **It is answered:** "I have pardoned, according to your word" (14:20).

3. **Recited in confession, as history:** "they stiffened their neck and appointed a leader to return to their slavery in Egypt. But you are a God ready to forgive, gracious and merciful, slow to anger" (Neh 9:17). **The name is now told as what God has shown himself to be through Israel's whole story.**
- **Where it comes from.** From **God's own mouth first** (Exo 34:6). Every human use goes back to that proclamation.

- **The name is used at once, in the next breath, to ask:** "pardon our iniquity and our sin" (Exo 34:9), with "for it is a stiff-necked people". **The name and the people's stiff neck are put side by side by Moses himself.** The same pairing returns in Neh 9:16–17.
- **The name includes its limit:** "but who will by no means clear the guilty" (Exo 34:7; Num 14:18). Moses quotes the limit too, and still pleads.
- **What it leads to.** Worship (Exo 34:8), pardon (Num 14:20), and confession (Neh 9).

- **Seat.** None in-verse. Neh 9:20 "your good Spirit to instruct them" is **God's, given** (divine; C v3 §1.6). **Pointer:** U1 §13 has Jonah using the same creed **against** God (Jon 4:2). With Moses and the Levites of Neh 9, **one creed is used three ways: worship, plea, and complaint.** Pilot §2.2 already notes the idiom shared between God and the wise (Pro 14:29 and others), and U1 §22 reads the human side of it.
- **(v2) Part B: Psa 86:15; 103:8; 145:8.** Three more uses of the name. Pilot §2.2 already lists all three as uses of the idiom.
- **An individual's plea against "insolent men":** "But you, O Lord, are a God merciful and gracious, slow to anger … Turn to me and be gracious to me" (Psa 86:14–16).

- **A recital with its reasoning:** "He will not always chide, nor will he keep his anger forever. He does not deal with us according to our sins" (103:9–10). This comes straight after "He made known his ways to Moses" (103:7). **The psalm names Moses as the one to whom the name was made known.**
- **Praise:** "The Lord is good to all, and his mercy is over all that he has made" (145:9).
- **The one creed is now used five ways:** worship (Exo 34:8), plea (Num 14; Psa 86), confession (Neh 9), complaint (Jonah, U1 §13) and praise (Psa 145).
- **Seat (v2).** **Outside:** Psa 86:13 "you have delivered my soul from the depths of Sheol". **The pleader's own. Genuine** (E v2 §10.1, §11.3).
- **(v3) Part C: Mic 7:18; Nah 1:3** (and the creed inside Joe 2:13, §56).

- "Who is a God like you, pardoning iniquity and passing over transgression …? He does not retain his anger forever, because he delights in steadfast love" (Mic 7:18); "you will cast all our sins into the depths of the sea" (7:19). **(#1892 pointer: read.)** This is the creed turned into a question of wonder.

- **Used against an enemy:** "The Lord is slow to anger and great in power, and the Lord will by no means clear the guilty" (Nah 1:3), against Nineveh. **The same words that Jonah complained were used to spare Nineveh (U1 §13) are here used to announce its end.**
## 6. Near the holy: wrath guarded against, and breaking out (HO) — Lev 10:6; Num 1:53; 18:5; 2Sa 6:7; 1Ch 13:10 · (v3) Eze 43:8

answer.not_an_observation: heading
answer.reason: the heading of a phenomenon, with the verses it covers

lines.text: - **The guard:** "the Levites shall camp around the tabernacle of the testimony, so that there may be no wrath on the congregation" (Num 1:53); "keep guard over the sanctuary and over the altar, that there may never again be wrath" (Num 18:5). **The guard is a people placed in a ring**, and "any outsider who comes near shall be put to death" (Num 1:51; 18:7).

- **Grief held back:** after Nadab and Abihu die, Aaron and his sons may not mourn: "Do not let the hair of your heads hang loose, and do not tear your clothes, lest you die, and wrath come upon all the congregation" (Lev 10:6). "And Aaron held his peace" (10:3). **The priest's own grief is withheld because of the holy.** The rest of Israel "may bewail the burning" (10:6).

- **The breaking out:** "Uzzah put out his hand to the ark of God and took hold of it, for the oxen stumbled. And the anger of the Lord was kindled against Uzzah" (2Sa 6:6–7; 1Ch 13:9–10). **The act was a reflex to steady the ark.**
- **The breaking out stops a celebration.** "David and all the house of Israel were celebrating before the Lord" (2Sa 6:5; 1Ch 13:8).

- **It produces anger at God, then fear of God.** "David was angry … David was afraid of the Lord that day … 'How can the ark of the Lord come to me?'" (2Sa 6:8–9; 1Ch 13:11–12). This is U1 §13 and §37.

- **(New here, from context.)** **The fear is resolved by seeing blessing on someone else.** "The Lord blessed Obed-edom and all his household … So David went and brought up the ark … with rejoicing" (2Sa 6:11–12). **David does not reason his way past the fear. He watches another household live with the ark.**
- **Seat.** None in-verse or in ±3. **Aaron "held his peace" (Lev 10:3) does the seat's work.** The grief is present, and it is not voiced.

- **(v3) Part C: Eze 43:8.** "setting their threshold by my threshold and their doorposts beside my doorposts, with only a wall between me and them. They have defiled my holy name … so I have consumed them in my anger." Then: "Now let them put away their whoring … and I will dwell in their midst forever" (43:9), and the temple is to be described "that they may be ashamed of their iniquities" (43:10).

answer.not_an_observation: heading
answer.reason: the heading of a phenomenon, with the verses it covers

lines.text: - **What it does.** It is warned of in advance (Lev 26; Deu 4–32; Jos 23) and narrated afterwards (Judg 2; 1Ki 11; 2Ki 17; 2Ch 28). **The same act appears as prediction and as history.**
- **Forgetting.** "take care lest you forget the Lord" (Deu 6:12); "You were unmindful of the Rock that bore you, and you forgot the God who gave you birth" (Deu 32:18).

- **Fullness.** "Jeshurun grew fat, and kicked; you grew fat, stout, and sleek; then he forsook God who made him" (Deu 32:15); "when … they have eaten and are full and grown fat, they will turn to other gods" (Deu 31:20). **Plenty comes before the turn.**

- **A deceived or turning heart.** "Take care lest your heart be deceived, and you turn aside" (Deu 11:16); "a man or woman … whose heart is turning away today" (Deu 29:18); Solomon's "heart had turned away" (1Ki 11:9), because "his wives turned away his heart" (1Ki 11:4).

- **False security in the heart.** The man who "blesses himself in his heart, saying, 'I shall be safe, though I walk in the stubbornness of my heart'" (Deu 29:19). **Here the anger is said to refuse forgiveness to one man, singled out:** "The Lord will not be willing to forgive him … the anger of the Lord and his jealousy will smoke against that man" (29:20).
- **Intermarriage.** "they would turn away your sons from following me" (Deu 7:4).

- **Distress.** "In the time of his distress he became yet more faithless to the Lord — this same King Ahaz. For he sacrificed to the gods of Damascus that had defeated him" (2Ch 28:22–23). **Distress drives Ahaz further from God, not back.** Contrast §16, where distress leads to crying out.

- **Stubbornness, and not believing.** "they would not listen, but were stubborn, as their fathers had been, who did not believe in the Lord their God" (2Ki 17:14); "I know how rebellious and stubborn you are" (Deu 31:27).

- **You become what you follow.** "They went after false idols and became false" (2Ki 17:15). In exile "you will serve gods of wood and stone … that neither see, nor hear, nor eat, nor smell" (Deu 4:28).

- **Walking contrary meets walking contrary.** "if … you will not listen to me, but walk contrary to me, then I will walk contrary to you in fury" (Lev 26:27–28). **The anger answers in the form of the provocation.** The next verses are the famine ("eat the flesh of your sons", 26:29) and "my soul will abhor you" (26:30). F v4 §4 reads this as mutual abhorrence.

- **What is known in the heart.** Joshua ties the threat to what the people already know: "you know in your hearts and souls, all of you, that not one word has failed of all the good things … so the Lord will bring upon you all the evil things" (Jos 23:14–15). **The heart's own knowledge of God's faithfulness is made the ground for believing the warning.**
- **The generation that did not know.** "there arose another generation after them who did not know the Lord or the work that he had done" (Judg 2:10), and they "provoked the Lord to anger" (2:12).

- **What it leads to.** Scattering, drought ("he will shut up the heavens", Deu 11:17), being given to plunderers, removal "out of his sight" (2Ki 17:18). Also **the hidden face** (Deu 32:20; 31:17–18; see §12).

answer.not_an_observation: heading
answer.reason: the heading of a phenomenon, with the verses it covers

lines.text: - "'Yet even now,' declares the Lord, 'return to me with all your heart, with fasting, with weeping, and with mourning; and rend your hearts and not your garments.' Return to the Lord your God, for he is gracious and merciful, slow to anger … Who knows whether he will not turn and relent, and leave a blessing behind him …?" (Joe 2:12–14).

- The king of Nineveh: "Let neither man nor beast … taste anything … let man and beast be covered with sackcloth, and let them call out mightily to God. Let everyone turn from his evil way and from the violence that is in his hands. Who knows? God may turn and relent and turn from his fierce anger, so that we may not perish" (Jon 3:7–9).
- **Fasting and the body**, and the heart: "rend your hearts and not your garments" (Joe 2:13). **Outward signs are not refused; the heart is named as what must be torn.**
- **Awe:** "the day of the Lord is great and very awesome; who can endure it?" (Joe 2:11).

- **What it leads to.** "When God saw what they did, how they turned from their evil way, God relented of the disaster" (Jon 3:10). **In Jonah the relenting is recorded.** In Joel it is left as "Who knows?"
- **In the verse:** Joe 2:13 "rend your hearts". **The hearers' own. Genuine** (A v3 §3.3; E v2 §10.1; C v3 §8.1, §8.5).
- **Outside:** Joe 2:12 "with all your heart" (A v3 §3.3; E v2 §1.9).
- Part B §43 had "It may be" (Jer 36:7). Part C §39 has "perhaps you may be hidden" (Zep 2:3).
- **Revisit of U1 §13.** Jonah's anger at God's mercy (Jon 4) follows this relenting. **The mercy he resented was given to a people who turned without knowing it would come.**
## 57. "I will bear the indignation, because I have sinned" (BE) — Mic 7:9

answer.not_an_observation: heading

lines.text: - **What it does.** "I will bear the indignation of the Lord because I have sinned against him, until he pleads my cause and executes judgment for me. He will bring me out to the light; I shall look upon his vindication" (Mic 7:9).
- **Where it comes from.** From **confessed sin**, and from **trust**: "But as for me, I will look to the Lord; I will wait for the God of my salvation; my God will hear me" (7:7).

- **Against the enemy's gloating:** "Rejoice not over me, O my enemy; when I fall, I shall rise; when I sit in darkness, the Lord will be a light to me" (7:8). The enemy said, "Where is the Lord your God?" (7:10).
- **What it leads to.** Vindication (7:10), then the confession of §5: "Who is a God like you …? He does not retain his anger forever" (7:18).
- Part B §28 asked "correct me, but not in anger". Job (§26) and Psalm 88 bore the anger without a cause.
- **Mic 7:9 bears it willingly, with a cause named** ("because I have sinned").
- **Lam 3:39 said the same from another side:** "Why should a living man complain … about the punishment of his sins?" (read as context in part B).
## 58. "Flee from the wrath to come": fruit, not presumption (FL) — Mat 3:7; Luk 3:7

And do not presume to say to yourselves, 'We have Abraham as our father,' for I tell you, God is able from these stones to raise up children for Abraham" (Mat 3:7–9; Luk 3:7–8).

lines.text: - "we all once lived in the passions of our flesh, carrying out the desires of the flesh and the mind, and were by nature children of wrath, like the rest of mankind. But God, being rich in mercy …" (Eph 2:3–4).
- "Since, therefore, we have now been justified by his blood, much more shall we be saved by him from the wrath of God" (Rom 5:9).
- "Jesus who delivers us from the wrath to come" (1Th 1:10).
- "God has not destined us for wrath, but to obtain salvation" (5:9).

- **Where it comes from.** From **God's love shown before any change in them**: "while we were still sinners, Christ died for us" (Rom 5:8); "even when we were dead in our trespasses, made us alive" (Eph 2:5).
- **A past remembered:** "In these you too once walked" (compare Col 3:7).
- **Turning and waiting:** "you turned to God from idols to serve the living and true God, and to wait for his Son from heaven" (1Th 1:9–10).
- **Soberness and hope:** "let us be sober, having put on the breastplate of faith and love, and for a helmet the hope of salvation" (5:8).
- **Joy:** "we also rejoice in God" (Rom 5:11).
- **Encouragement of others:** "Therefore encourage one another and build one another up" (1Th 5:11).
- **Reconciliation:** "if while we were enemies we were reconciled to God" (Rom 5:10).
- **In the verse:** Eph 2:3 "flesh" ×2. **The speaker's and the readers' own former way of life. Genuine** (A v3 §2.2; B v3 §1.8; C v3 §1.11).
- **Outside:** Eph 2:2 "the spirit that is now at work in the sons of disobedience". **A hostile spirit** (H v1 §1.6; C v3 §9.8, §11).
- **Isa 12:1 (§30) spoke of the anger as turned away for one person. §60 is the first group that speaks of a wrath still to come as one they are delivered from, while it remains certain for others.**

Part C shows that two verses earlier, God's wrath is named as coming on these things** (3:6). **The human anger to be put off (3:8) stands two verses after the divine wrath that comes (3:6).** Revisit note for U1 §25 at consolidation.
## 64. The wrath finished: bowls, winepress, and the song of the conquerors (FW) — Rev 14:19; 15:1; 15:7; 16:1; 19:15

answer.not_an_observation: heading
answer.reason: the heading of a phenomenon, with the verses it covers

lines.text: - "the great winepress of the wrath of God" (Rev 14:19); "seven angels with seven plagues, which are the last, for with them the wrath of God is finished" (15:1).
- "seven golden bowls full of the wrath of God" (15:7); "Go and pour out on the earth the seven bowls of the wrath of God" (16:1).
- "He will tread the winepress of the fury of the wrath of God the Almighty" (19:15).
- **Where it comes from.** From **the worship of the beast**: "harmful and painful sores came upon the people who bore the mark of the beast and worshiped its image" (16:2).

- **The conquerors sing:** "those who had conquered the beast … standing beside the sea of glass with harps of God … sing the song of Moses, the servant of God, and the song of the Lamb, saying, 'Great and amazing are your deeds, O Lord God the Almighty! Just and true are your ways'" (15:2–3). **Those who have come through confess that the wrath is just.**
- **No one can enter:** "no one could enter the sanctuary until the seven plagues of the seven angels were finished" (15:8).
- **What it leads to.** "It is done!" (16:17); the Word of God on the white horse, "King of kings" (19:13–16).
- **Seat.** None in-verse. **Outside:** Rev 16:3 "every living thing" (*psyche*). **Life-sense** (G v3 §0).

- **Isa 63:3 (§41): "I have trodden the winepress alone."** Rev 14:19 and 19:15 take up the winepress. In Isaiah no one helped; in Revelation "the armies of heaven … were following him" (19:14). Pointer only.
- **"The song of Moses" (Rev 15:3).** Part A began with the song of the delivered at the sea (Exo 15:7, §3). **Unit 2 ends with the same kind of song, sung by those who conquered.**

1. **Part A: seven of the nine are genuine.** Num 11:33 is spurious and Job 4:9 is divine. Six of the seven are a particular person's seat: three are Hezekiah's own heart in his two episodes (2Ch 29:10; 32:25–26), one is the provoker's heart (Solomon), one is the receiving spirit (Job), and one is another person's glad heart (Aaron). The seventh, Num 16:22, is God's relation to every human spirit.

- **Part A:** Num 32:7, 9 (the people's heart discouraged by the spies, which provoked the anger). **Correction:** v1 also listed 2Ki 23:25 as new, but E v2 §6 has it. v1's citation finder did not resolve shorthand references; v2 used a finder that does, and re-checked every part-A "new" and "not found" claim.
- **(v2) Part B:**
- Psa 6:3 (the chastened man's troubled soul)
- Psa 30:3 (the soul brought up from Sheol)
- Isa 13:7 (every heart melting on the day)
- Isa 47:7 (Babylon not laying it to heart)
- Jer 30:21 (the prince who pledges his heart to approach)
- **(v3) Part C:** Eze 21:15 (hearts melting before the sword). Rom 13:5 is an **in-verse** seat new as a reading (§66 point 4).

- **(v3) The citation finder was corrected again.** It had misread "13:13, 19:12" as verse 19 of chapter 13. After the fix, every "new" and "not found" claim in parts A, B and C was re-run. **All the part-A and part-B claims above still hold.** A plain-text search for the chapter:verse strings was also run as a second check; it found no other hits.

- **Unit 1 §13 (AG) and §37.** The Uzzah sequence gains its end from context (2Sa 6:11–12). **David's fear of God resolves when he sees the Lord bless Obed-edom's household, and he brings the ark up "with rejoicing".** Revisit note for U1 §13 when unit 1 and unit 2 are consolidated.

findings.text: What it does: Abraham: "Oh let not the Lord be angry, and I will speak. Suppose thirty are found there" (Gen 18:30), and at the last: "Oh let not the Lord be angry, and I will speak again but this once. Suppose ten" (18:32); Gideon, after the fleece was wet: "Let not your anger burn against me; let me speak just once more. Please let me test just once more with the fleece" (Judg 6:39); The same form appears in two different kinds of asking. Abraham asks for a city he does not belong to. Gideon asks for assurance for himself.

Where it comes from. From knowing the distance and asking anyway. Abraham says twice, "I have undertaken to speak to the Lord, I who am but dust and ashes" (Gen 18:27; 18:31). Gideon has already had his sign (Judg 6:38). The asker knows that the request presses on God's patience.

How it co-exists: Boldness and restraint in one sentence. The plea not to anger does not stop the asking. It is what allows the asking; Every request is granted, and no anger comes. "I will not do it, if I find thirty there" (Gen 18:30); "God did so that night" (Judg 6:40). The anger feared never appears in either passage.
What it leads to. The asker stops. Abraham stops at ten and "returned to his place" (Gen 18:33). The asker, not God, sets the limit ("but this once").

Seat. None in-verse or in ±3. The self-description "dust and ashes" (Gen 18:27) does the seat's work: the asker places himself before God as creature. Job repents "in dust and ashes" (Job 42:6), read in §25 of this document. Pointer only: the phrase links the bold asker and the humbled sufferer.

What it does. Two different occasions: At the call: "Oh, my Lord, please send someone else." "Then the anger of the Lord was kindled against Moses" (Exo 4:13–14). The anger is answered at once by provision: Aaron "is coming out to meet you, and when he sees you, he will be glad in his heart" (4:14); "I will be with your mouth and with his mouth" (4:15); At the end: "Even with me the Lord was angry on your account and said, 'You also shall not go in there'" (Deu 1:37); "the Lord was angry with me because of you and would not listen to me … 'Enough from you; do not speak to me of this matter again'" (3:26); "I must die in this land; I must not go over the Jordan" (4:21–22).

Where it comes from: Exo 4: the servant's refusal of the call; Deuteronomy: "on your account" / "because of you", three times (Deu 1:37; 3:26; 4:21). Moses traces the anger at himself to the people. The leader bears God's anger as the people's leader, and says so.

How it co-exists: The plea refused, and something else given instead. Moses "pleaded with the Lord" (Deu 3:23–25). The answer was "Enough", then "lift up your eyes … and look at it with your eyes" (3:27). The land is given to the eye, not the foot; The anger is followed each time by a charge to hand on: "Encourage him" (Deu 1:38); "charge Joshua, and encourage and strengthen him" (3:28). In Exo 4 a partner is given, and in Deuteronomy a successor. The anger does not end the man's service. It reshapes it.

What it leads to. Moses speaks of his exclusion to the people as a warning to them. Deu 4:21–22 is followed at once by "Take care, lest you forget the covenant" (4:23) and "the Lord your God is a consuming fire" (4:24). His own bearing of the anger becomes his teaching.

Seat: In the verse: Exo 4:14 "glad in his heart". The other party's (Aaron's). Genuine. Already read in G v3 §13.2 ("the heart goes out to meet"). Read from the M02 side, it shows that the anger at Moses is met with a glad heart coming towards him; Outside the verse: none in Deu 1:34–40; 3:23–29; 4:18–25.

Part B: Psa 106:32. "They angered him at the waters of Meribah, and it went ill with Moses on their account, for they made his spirit bitter, and he spoke rashly with his lips" (Psa 106:32–33): The psalm gives an inner route for the "because of you" that Moses spoke of in Deuteronomy. The people's provocation reaches a spirit, and Moses' rash speech follows; Whose spirit is not determinable. The M47 spirit classification v2 marks Psa 106:33 as [U] (#1880 item C-R4; C v3 R4). It could be Moses' spirit embittered, or God's Spirit rebelled against (compare Isa 63:10). Either way, the verse ties Meribah to Moses' loss "on their account".

What it does: Sung by the rescued: "you send out your fury; it consumes them like stubble" (Exo 15:7); Promised to the obedient: "if you carefully obey his voice … then I will be an enemy to your enemies and an adversary to your adversaries" (Exo 23:22); Released by the cry of the weak: "If you do mistreat them, and they cry out to me, I will surely hear their cry, and my wrath will burn" (Exo 22:23–24); Released by the psalmist's call: "In my distress I called upon the Lord … my cry came to his ears. Then the earth reeled … because he was angry" (2Sa 22:7–8).

Where it comes from. From the human cry: the widow's and orphan's (Exo 22:23), the poor debtor's (22:27: "if he cries to me, I will hear, for I am compassionate"), David's "in my distress" (2Sa 22:7). In two of the four verses, the human cry is what precedes the anger.

How it co-exists: The enemy's own appetite. In the song, the enemy boasts, "my desire [nephesh] shall have its fill of them" (Exo 15:9), and is answered by the wind of God (15:10). The enemy's appetite and God's fury meet over the same people. Already read in F v4 §8.4 ("the enemy's soul and the pursued soul"); The same anger threatens the one it protects, if roles reverse. Exo 22:24 is said to Israel about their own widows: "I will kill you with the sword, and your wives shall become widows". God's anger is for the weak, whoever the oppressor is.
What it leads to. Praise (Exo 15), or deliverance (2Sa 22:17 onward, not read here).
Seat. None in-verse. Outside: Exo 15:9 nephesh (the enemy's, appetite-sense) and 15:8, 10 "blast", "wind", "heart of the sea" (not inner-being). F v4 §8.4 covers 15:9. Nothing new.

Part B: Psa 7:11; 18:7; 21:9; 78:49; 78:50; 110:5; Isa 30:27; 30:30; 66:14; 66:15: Psa 18:7 is the psalm text of 2Sa 22:8: "In my distress I called upon the Lord … because he was angry" (Psa 18:6–7); The upright in heart, and the call to repent. "God is a righteous judge, and a God who feels indignation every day" (Psa 7:11). This follows "you who test the minds and hearts … who saves the upright in heart" (7:9–10), and is followed by "If a man does not repent, God will whet his sword" (7:12). The protection is for the upright in heart, and the indignation waits on repentance; The king who trusts: "the king trusts in the Lord … Your hand will find out all your enemies" (Psa 21:7–9). The king at God's right hand: "Your people will offer themselves freely" (110:3, 5); The Exodus retold: "He made a path for his anger; he did not spare them from death" (Psa 78:50). "Then he led out his people like sheep" (78:52); The protected rejoice in the heart; "You shall have a song … and gladness of heart" (Isa 30:29), while "the Assyrians will be terror-stricken" (30:31); "As one whom his mother comforts, so I will comfort you … You shall see, and your heart shall rejoice; your bones shall flourish like the grass" (66:13–14); The protected are the people the anger struck earlier: "the Lord binds up the brokenness of his people, and heals the wounds inflicted by his blow" (Isa 30:26); Seat ; In the verse: Isa 66:14 "your heart shall rejoice". The comforted people's own. Genuine. Psa 78:50 "them" (nephesh) is the Egyptians' life. Life-sense; Outside: Psa 7:9–10 "hearts" / "upright in heart". Isa 30:29 "gladness of heart"; What part B adds. Part A had only praise (Exo 15). Part B places the joy of the protected in the heart.

Part C: Eze 36:6; Nah 1:2; Hab 3:8; 3:12; Zec 8:2: Anger for the reproached: "Behold, I have spoken in my jealous wrath, because you have suffered the reproach of the nations" (Eze 36:6). Edom took the land "with wholehearted joy and utter contempt" (36:5). "you will soon come home" (36:8); "I am jealous for Zion with great jealousy, and I am jealous for her with great wrath. … I have returned to Zion" (Zec 8:2–3). "The Lord … keeps wrath for his enemies" (Nah 1:2); Habakkuk's prayer, from inside the fear:; "O Lord, I have heard the report of you, and your work, O Lord, do I fear … in wrath remember mercy" (Hab 3:2); "Was your wrath against the rivers …? … You went out for the salvation of your people" (3:8, 13); the enemy came "rejoicing as if to devour the poor in secret" (3:14); then: "I hear, and my body trembles; my lips quiver … rottenness enters into my bones … Yet I will quietly wait for the day of trouble to come upon people who invade us" (3:16); and: "Though the fig tree should not blossom … yet I will rejoice in the Lord" (3:17–18).

What it does: God himself leaves the door open: "Now therefore let me alone, that my wrath may burn hot against them" (Exo 32:10). The anger waits on whether Moses will let God alone; Moses argues. He argues from ownership: "why does your wrath burn hot against your people, whom you have brought out" (32:11). He argues from God's reputation: "Why should the Egyptians say, 'With evil intent did he bring them out'?" (32:12). He argues from promise: "Remember Abraham, Isaac, and Israel" (32:13); He argues from justice between the one and the many: "O God, the God of the spirits of all flesh, shall one man sin, and will you be angry with all the congregation?" (Num 16:22); With the body: "I lay prostrate before the Lord … forty days and forty nights. I neither ate bread nor drank water" (Deu 9:18); For the particular man: "the Lord was so angry with Aaron that he was ready to destroy him. And I prayed for Aaron also" (Deu 9:20).

Where it comes from. From fear. "For I was afraid of the anger and hot displeasure that the Lord bore against you" (Deu 9:19). The intercessor's own fear of God's anger drives the plea for others. It does not stop it.

How it co-exists: Intercession sits alongside the intercessor's own anger. The same chapter has Moses' own anger breaking the tablets. Moses is angry at the people and pleads for them against God's anger, within one episode; It is answered: "the Lord relented" (Exo 32:14); "the Lord listened to me that time also" (Deu 9:19).

What it leads to. The people are spared. In Deuteronomy, the memory of the intercession is itself turned into instruction (Deu 9:25–29, "So I lay prostrate …"), set against the people's claim to righteousness.

Seat: In the verse: Num 16:22 "spirits of all flesh". God's relation to every human spirit, given as the ground of the plea. Genuine. Nothing new; Outside: none in Exo 32:7–15; Deu 9:15–22; Pointer: the fasting body (Deu 9:18) does the seat's work here, as the face and bed do in U1 §1.

Part B: Psa 106:23. "Therefore he said he would destroy them — had not Moses, his chosen one, stood in the breach before him, to turn away his wrath from destroying them.": The psalm names Moses' intercession (Exo 32; Deu 9) "standing in the breach". Its context is "They forgot God, their Savior" (106:21); Part B also shows intercession forbidden and absent:; forbidden: "As for you, do not pray for this people … do not intercede with me, for I will not hear you"; absent: "there was no one to intercede"; repaid with evil: Jer 18:20.

Part C: Eze 9:8; Dan 9:16; Zec 1:12: The prophet refused. "while they were striking, and I was left alone, I fell upon my face, and cried, 'Ah, Lord God! Will you destroy all the remnant of Israel …?'" (Eze 9:8). The answer is no: "The guilt … is exceedingly great … For they say, 'The Lord has forsaken the land, and the Lord does not see.' As for me, my eye will not spare" (9:9–10). Some are spared: the mark is put "on the foreheads of the men who sigh and groan over all the abominations" (9:4, context read). Those who grieve over the sin are marked. The one who pleads for the rest is not answered; Daniel's confession-intercession:; "O Lord, according to all your righteous acts, let your anger and your wrath turn away from your city Jerusalem … because for our sins, and for the iniquities of our fathers, Jerusalem … [has] become a byword" (Dan 9:16); "the Lord our God is righteous in all the works that he has done" (9:14); "for your own sake" (9:17); "we do not present our pleas before you because of our righteousness, but because of your great mercy" (9:18); An angel intercedes: "O Lord of hosts, how long will you have no mercy on Jerusalem …, against which you have been angry these seventy years?" This is answered with "gracious and comforting words" (Zec 1:12–13).

What it does. Three moments: Proclaimed and received: "The Lord, the Lord, a God merciful and gracious, slow to anger" (Exo 34:6). Moses "quickly bowed his head toward the earth and worshiped" (34:8); Pleaded back: Moses quotes it to God word for word as his argument: "'The Lord is slow to anger and abounding in steadfast love …' Please pardon the iniquity of this people" (Num 14:18–19). It is answered: "I have pardoned, according to your word" (14:20); Recited in confession, as history: "they stiffened their neck and appointed a leader to return to their slavery in Egypt. But you are a God ready to forgive, gracious and merciful, slow to anger" (Neh 9:17). The name is now told as what God has shown himself to be through Israel's whole story.
Where it comes from. From God's own mouth first (Exo 34:6). Every human use goes back to that proclamation.

How it co-exists: The name is used at once, in the next breath, to ask: "pardon our iniquity and our sin" (Exo 34:9), with "for it is a stiff-necked people". The name and the people's stiff neck are put side by side by Moses himself. The same pairing returns in Neh 9:16–17; The name includes its limit: "but who will by no means clear the guilty" (Exo 34:7; Num 14:18). Moses quotes the limit too, and still pleads.
What it leads to. Worship (Exo 34:8), pardon (Num 14:20), and confession (Neh 9).

Seat. None in-verse. Neh 9:20 "your good Spirit to instruct them" is God's, given. Pointer: U1 §13 has Jonah using the same creed against God (Jon 4:2). With Moses and the Levites of Neh 9, one creed is used three ways: worship, plea, and complaint. Pilot §2.2 already notes the idiom shared between God and the wise (Pro 14:29 and others), and U1 §22 reads the human side of it.

Part B: Psa 86:15; 103:8; 145:8. Three more uses of the name. Pilot §2.2 already lists all three as uses of the idiom: An individual's plea against "insolent men": "But you, O Lord, are a God merciful and gracious, slow to anger … Turn to me and be gracious to me" (Psa 86:14–16); A recital with its reasoning: "He will not always chide, nor will he keep his anger forever. He does not deal with us according to our sins" (103:9–10). This comes straight after "He made known his ways to Moses" (103:7). The psalm names Moses as the one to whom the name was made known; Praise: "The Lord is good to all, and his mercy is over all that he has made" (145:9); The one creed is now used five ways: worship (Exo 34:8), plea (Num 14; Psa 86), confession (Neh 9), complaint and praise (Psa 145); Seat . Outside: Psa 86:13 "you have delivered my soul from the depths of Sheol". The pleader's own. Genuine.

Part C: Mic 7:18; Nah 1:3: "Who is a God like you, pardoning iniquity and passing over transgression …? He does not retain his anger forever, because he delights in steadfast love" (Mic 7:18); "you will cast all our sins into the depths of the sea" (7:19). (#1892 pointer: read.) This is the creed turned into a question of wonder; Used against an enemy: "The Lord is slow to anger and great in power, and the Lord will by no means clear the guilty" (Nah 1:3), against Nineveh. The same words that Jonah complained were used to spare Nineveh are here used to announce its end; The creed is now used eight ways: worship, plea, confession, complaint, praise, wonder (Micah), the announcement of judgment (Nahum), and the ground for returning.

What it does: The guard: "the Levites shall camp around the tabernacle of the testimony, so that there may be no wrath on the congregation" (Num 1:53); "keep guard over the sanctuary and over the altar, that there may never again be wrath" (Num 18:5). The guard is a people placed in a ring, and "any outsider who comes near shall be put to death" (Num 1:51; 18:7); Grief held back: after Nadab and Abihu die, Aaron and his sons may not mourn: "Do not let the hair of your heads hang loose, and do not tear your clothes, lest you die, and wrath come upon all the congregation" (Lev 10:6). "And Aaron held his peace" (10:3). The priest's own grief is withheld because of the holy. The rest of Israel "may bewail the burning" (10:6); The breaking out: "Uzzah put out his hand to the ark of God and took hold of it, for the oxen stumbled. And the anger of the Lord was kindled against Uzzah" (2Sa 6:6–7; 1Ch 13:9–10). The act was a reflex to steady the ark.

How it co-exists: The breaking out stops a celebration. "David and all the house of Israel were celebrating before the Lord" (2Sa 6:5; 1Ch 13:8); It produces anger at God, then fear of God. "David was angry … David was afraid of the Lord that day … 'How can the ark of the Lord come to me?'" (2Sa 6:8–9; 1Ch 13:11–12). This is U1 §13 and §37; (New here, from context.) The fear is resolved by seeing blessing on someone else. "The Lord blessed Obed-edom and all his household … So David went and brought up the ark … with rejoicing" (2Sa 6:11–12). David does not reason his way past the fear. He watches another household live with the ark.
Seat. None in-verse or in ±3. Aaron "held his peace" (Lev 10:3) does the seat's work. The grief is present, and it is not voiced.

Part C: Eze 43:8. "setting their threshold by my threshold and their doorposts beside my doorposts, with only a wall between me and them. They have defiled my holy name … so I have consumed them in my anger." Then: "Now let them put away their whoring … and I will dwell in their midst forever" (43:9), and the temple is to be described "that they may be ashamed of their iniquities" (43:10): Part A's nearness was a danger of approach (Uzzah). Here the nearness is profaned by building one's own house against God's. The remedy is a new dwelling and shame.
What it does. It is warned of in advance (Lev 26; Deu 4–32; Jos 23) and narrated afterwards (Judg 2; 1Ki 11; 2Ki 17; 2Ch 28). The same act appears as prediction and as history.
findings.flag: verse taken from the section heading: the claim's references are bare

findings.text: Where it comes from. This is where the texts give most. The roots named in the context of these verses: Forgetting. "take care lest you forget the Lord" (Deu 6:12); "You were unmindful of the Rock that bore you, and you forgot the God who gave you birth" (Deu 32:18); Fullness. "Jeshurun grew fat, and kicked; you grew fat, stout, and sleek; then he forsook God who made him" (Deu 32:15); "when … they have eaten and are full and grown fat, they will turn to other gods" (Deu 31:20). Plenty comes before the turn; A deceived or turning heart. "Take care lest your heart be deceived, and you turn aside" (Deu 11:16); "a man or woman … whose heart is turning away today" (Deu 29:18); Solomon's "heart had turned away" (1Ki 11:9), because "his wives turned away his heart" (1Ki 11:4); False security in the heart. The man who "blesses himself in his heart, saying, 'I shall be safe, though I walk in the stubbornness of my heart'" (Deu 29:19). Here the anger is said to refuse forgiveness to one man, singled out: "The Lord will not be willing to forgive him … the anger of the Lord and his jealousy will smoke against that man" (29:20); Intermarriage. "they would turn away your sons from following me" (Deu 7:4); Distress. "In the time of his distress he became yet more faithless to the Lord — this same King Ahaz. For he sacrificed to the gods of Damascus that had defeated him" (2Ch 28:22–23). Distress drives Ahaz further from God, not back. Contrast §16, where distress leads to crying out; Stubbornness, and not believing. "they would not listen, but were stubborn, as their fathers had been, who did not believe in the Lord their God" (2Ki 17:14); "I know how rebellious and stubborn you are" (Deu 31:27).

How it co-exists: You become what you follow. "They went after false idols and became false" (2Ki 17:15). In exile "you will serve gods of wood and stone … that neither see, nor hear, nor eat, nor smell" (Deu 4:28); Walking contrary meets walking contrary. "if … you will not listen to me, but walk contrary to me, then I will walk contrary to you in fury" (Lev 26:27–28). The anger answers in the form of the provocation. The next verses are the famine ("eat the flesh of your sons", 26:29) and "my soul will abhor you" (26:30). F v4 §4 reads this as mutual abhorrence; What is known in the heart. Joshua ties the threat to what the people already know: "you know in your hearts and souls, all of you, that not one word has failed of all the good things … so the Lord will bring upon you all the evil things" (Jos 23:14–15). The heart's own knowledge of God's faithfulness is made the ground for believing the warning; The generation that did not know. "there arose another generation after them who did not know the Lord or the work that he had done" (Judg 2:10), and they "provoked the Lord to anger" (2:12).
What it leads to. Scattering, drought ("he will shut up the heavens", Deu 11:17), being given to plunderers, removal "out of his sight" (2Ki 17:18). Also the hidden face.

Seat: In the verse: 1Ki 11:9 "his heart had turned away". Solomon's own. Genuine, the cause. Already read in A v3 §2.2 and pilot §2 ("the heart that provokes the anger"); Outside the verse (all genuine unless noted):; Deu 11:16 "lest your heart be deceived" (before) and 11:18 "lay up these words of mine in your heart and in your soul" (after). The deceived heart is the cause; the heart filled with the words is the guard. B v3 §4.1; C v3 §8.2; E v2 §4.1; G v3 §10; H v1 §5.1; Deu 29:18–19 "whose heart is turning away" / "blesses himself in his heart … stubbornness of my heart". E v2 §4.1, §12; C v3 §9.1; F v4 §9.6. Pilot §1.6 reads 29:20 with it; 1Ki 11:4 "his wives turned away his heart … his heart was not wholly true"; Jos 23:14 "you know in your hearts and souls". B v3 §1.1 ("the heart as the knower"); Lev 26:29–30 "flesh" (bodily) and "my soul will abhor you"; Nothing new in the seat itself. What part A adds is how regularly the heart is named in the verses around the anger verse, and not in the anger verse itself. Pilot §2 had said that the "anger was kindled" series carries "the human inner cause by narrative". Part A confirms this, and finds that the seat is named nearby, in warnings and explanations.

Part B: Psa 78:58, 78:59, 78:62; Isa 65:3; Jer 7:18, 7:19, 7:20; 11:17; 15:14; 17:4; 25:6, 25:7; 32:29, 32:30, 32:31, 32:32 (16 verses): More roots; Treachery like the fathers': "turned away and acted treacherously like their fathers; they twisted like a deceitful bow" (Psa 78:57); Self-holiness: "who say, 'Keep to yourself, do not come near me, for I am too holy for you'" (Isa 65:5). This is said to a God who says "I spread out my hands all the day to a rebellious people" (65:2); Trust in man: "Cursed is the man who trusts in man and makes flesh his strength, whose heart turns away from the Lord" (Jer 17:5); From youth, turning the back: "done nothing but evil in my sight from their youth" (Jer 32:30); "They have turned to me their back and not their face … they have not listened to receive instruction" (32:33); Whole households, all ranks: "The children gather wood, the fathers kindle fire, and the women knead dough … to provoke me to anger" (Jer 7:18); "their kings and their officials, their priests and their prophets" (32:32); The provocation turns on the provoker. "Is it I whom they provoke? declares the Lord. Is it not themselves, to their own shame?" (Jer 7:19); "that you might provoke me to anger with the work of your hands to your own harm" (25:7); Pilot §2 lists Jer 7 in the ka'as series; What part B adds is the text's own statement that the provoking harms the provoker. Part A had "they … became false" (2Ki 17:15). Jeremiah adds "to their own shame" and "to your own harm"; Seat . Outside: Jer 17:5 "whose heart turns away". Genuine. Nothing new.

Part C: Eze 8:17; 8:18; 20:28; Hos 8:5; 12:14: "Is it too light a thing …? … they put the branch to their nose" (Eze 8:17), with "their backs to the temple of the Lord, and their faces toward the east, worshiping the sun" (8:16); Prayer refused: "And though they cry in my ears with a loud voice, I will not hear them" (8:18); God's own "how long?": "How long will they be incapable of innocence?" (Hos 8:5). The question the laments ask of God is asked by God of the people; "Will you defile yourselves after the manner of your fathers …?" (Eze 20:30); "Ephraim has given bitter provocation" (Hos 12:14).

What it does: Complaint: "the people complained in the hearing of the Lord about their misfortunes, and when the Lord heard it, his anger was kindled" (Num 11:1); Craving: "While the meat was yet between their teeth … the anger of the Lord was kindled" (Num 11:33). The place is named after it: "there they buried the people who had the craving" (11:34). Already read in A v3 §2.2 ("craving and anger"); Unbelief: "Yet in spite of this word you did not believe the Lord your God … And the Lord heard your words and was angered" (Deu 1:32–34); Discouraging the heart: the spies "discouraged the heart of the people of Israel from going into the land" (Num 32:9), and "the Lord's anger was kindled on that day" (32:10).

Where it comes from: From ingratitude after being carried: "the Lord your God carried you, as a man carries his son … Yet … you did not believe" (Deu 1:31–32); From not following wholly: "because they have not wholly followed me, none except Caleb … and Joshua … for they have wholly followed the Lord" (Num 32:11–12).

How it co-exists: The provocation is inherited. "you have risen in your fathers' place, a brood of sinful men, to increase still more the fierce anger of the Lord" (Num 32:14). The sons are warned that they are repeating the fathers. They answer by offering to go armed before their brothers (32:16–17); Remembering is commanded against self-righteousness. "Do not say in your heart … 'It is because of my righteousness'" (Deu 9:4); "Remember and do not forget how you provoked the Lord your God to wrath in the wilderness" (9:7). Memory of provoking God is the cure for the heart's claim to righteousness; Moses caught between. In Num 11:10–15 Moses hears the weeping, is "displeased", and says: "Why have you dealt ill with your servant? … kill me at once … that I may not see my wretchedness" (11:11, 15). The leader between God's anger and the people's complaint asks to die.

What it leads to. Fire, plague, forty years of wandering "until all the generation that had done evil … was gone" (Num 32:13), and a list of place names that keeps the memory: "At Taberah also, and at Massah and at Kibroth-hattaavah you provoked the Lord to wrath" (Deu 9:22).

Seat: In the verse: Num 11:33 "meat" (basar). Spurious. Pilot §0 lists it among the links that do not count; Outside: Num 32:7, 9 "discourage the heart of the people". The people's own heart, as what the spies weakened. Genuine. Deu 9:4–5 "Do not say in your heart … the uprightness of your heart". Genuine. Num 32:7, 9 is not cited in any batch. New as an M02 context seat: discouraging the heart of others is what provokes the anger.

Part B: Psa 78:21, 78:31; 95:11: Psalm 78 retells the wilderness:; "Can God spread a table in the wilderness?" (78:19), answered by anger "because they did not believe in God and did not trust his saving power" (78:22); "before they had satisfied their craving, while the food was still in their mouths, the anger of God rose" (78:30–31); "In spite of all this, they still sinned … So he made their days vanish like a breath, and their years in terror" (78:32–33); Psa 95:11: "I swore in my wrath, 'They shall not enter my rest'", after "They are a people who go astray in their heart" (95:10). Part B's form of "remember" is a psalm that is sung, so that the hearers "do not harden your hearts"; Seat . Psa 95:10 "heart". Nothing new. Psa 78:37 "heart" is read under §33.

Part C: Heb 3:10; 3:11; 3:17; 4:3: Hebrews reads Psalm 95 to a new audience:; "Take care, brothers, lest there be in any of you an evil, unbelieving heart, leading you to fall away from the living God. But exhort one another every day, as long as it is called 'today,' that none of you may be hardened by the deceitfulness of sin" (Heb 3:12–13); "So we see that they were unable to enter because of unbelief" (3:19); "let us fear lest any of you should seem to have failed to reach it" (4:1); "we who have believed enter that rest" (4:3); The wilderness provocation is made a daily warning, kept by exhorting one another — part A's "remember and do not forget" (Deu 9:7) in a new form; Seat ; In the verse: Heb 3:10 "go astray in their heart". The fathers'. Genuine; Outside: Heb 3:8, 15 "do not harden your hearts"; 3:12 "evil, unbelieving heart".

What it does: Spoken against: "Why then were you not afraid to speak against my servant Moses?" And the anger of the Lord was kindled against them (Num 12:8–9). The charge is a lack of fear; Silenced: Amaziah to the prophet: "Have we made you a royal counselor? Stop! Why should you be struck down?" (2Ch 25:16). The prophet stops, but says: "I know that God has determined to destroy you, because you have done this and have not listened to my counsel."; Killed: after Jehoiada died, "the king listened to them [the princes]"; prophets "testified against them, but they would not pay attention"; Zechariah, whom "the Spirit of God clothed", was stoned "in the court of the house of the Lord" (2Ch 24:17–21).

Where it comes from: From rivalry (Miriam and Aaron, Num 12:1–2, not read here); From loss of the restraining figure: "after the death of Jehoiada the princes … paid homage to the king. Then the king listened to them" (2Ch 24:17); From pride after victory: Amaziah worships "the gods of a people who did not deliver their own people from your hand" (2Ch 25:15).
How it co-exists. Aaron confesses at once: "Oh, my lord, do not punish us because we have done foolishly and have sinned" (Num 12:11). Amaziah does not.
What it leads to. Leprosy and intercession (Num 12:10–13), stoning (2Ch 24:21), and a determined end (2Ch 25:16).
Seat. None in-verse. 2Ch 24:20 "Spirit of God clothed Zechariah". God's, given. Divine. Num 12:12 "flesh" is bodily.

Part C: 1Th 2:16. "who killed both the Lord Jesus and the prophets, and drove us out … by hindering us from speaking to the Gentiles that they might be saved — so as always to fill up the measure of their sins. But wrath has come upon them at last!" (1Th 2:15–16): The messenger spurned now includes hindering the message from reaching others; The same passage has Paul "torn away from you … in person not in heart".

What it does: Atonement carried into the plague: "Take your censer … carry it quickly to the congregation and make atonement for them, for wrath has gone out from the Lord" (Num 16:46). Aaron "ran into the midst … And he stood between the dead and the living, and the plague was stopped" (16:47–48). The priest's body stands on the line; Execution of the leaders: "hang them in the sun before the Lord, that the fierce anger of the Lord may turn away from Israel" (Num 25:4). Then Phinehas's spear (25:7), read in U1 §15 (SP, 25:11); Nothing of the devoted thing kept: "None of the devoted things shall stick to your hand, that the Lord may turn from the fierceness of his anger and show you mercy and have compassion on you" (Deu 13:17).
Where it comes from. From the command (Num 25:4; Deu 13) or the leader's urgency (Num 16:46: "carry it quickly").
How it co-exists. Weeping and zeal in one scene. The people are "weeping in the entrance of the tent of meeting" (Num 25:6) while the offender walks past with a Midianite woman, and Phinehas acts.
What it leads to. The plague stops; the anger turns; mercy and compassion are promised in the same verse as the purging (Deu 13:17).

Part B: Psa 106:29. "Then Phinehas stood up and intervened, and the plague was stayed. And that was counted to him as righteousness from generation to generation forever" (106:30–31). The psalm adds the verdict on the act: it was counted as righteousness.

What it does. "God's anger was kindled because he went, and the angel of the Lord took his stand in the way as his adversary" (Num 22:22). "The donkey saw the angel … And Balaam struck the donkey" (22:23, 25).
Where it comes from. From going after a permission hedged with "only do what I tell you" (22:20).
How it co-exists. Balaam's own anger at the donkey falls on the creature that saved him. Balaam is angry at the donkey while God is angry at Balaam, and only the donkey sees it.
What it leads to. Not read past 22:25 here. U1 has Balaam at Num 23:7–8.

What it does: Outsiders ask: "the next generation … and the foreigner who comes from a far land, will say … 'Why has the Lord done thus to this land? What caused the heat of this great anger?'" (Deu 29:22, 24); An answer is given: "It is because they abandoned the covenant of the Lord" (29:25), "Therefore the anger of the Lord was kindled against this land" (29:27), "and the Lord uprooted them from their land in anger and fury and great wrath … as they are this day" (29:28); The sufferers ask: "they will say in that day, 'Have not these evils come upon us because our God is not among us?'" (Deu 31:17). The people read their trouble as God's absence; A king reads it to his people: "the wrath of the Lord came on Judah and Jerusalem … as you see with your own eyes" (2Ch 29:8); Exiles explain it to foreign officials: "because our fathers had angered the God of heaven, he gave them into the hand of Nebuchadnezzar" (Ezr 5:12).
Where it comes from. From seeing. "as you see with your own eyes" (2Ch 29:8); "when they see the afflictions of that land" (Deu 29:22).

How it co-exists: A limit on reading. "The secret things belong to the Lord our God, but the things that are revealed belong to us and to our children forever, that we may do all the words of this law" (Deu 29:29). Read straight after the explanation of the ruin, this sets the reading of God's anger inside what is revealed, and turns it to doing; A song as witness. "write this song and teach it … that this song may be a witness for me against the people of Israel" (Deu 31:19). The explanation is given before the ruin, so that the ruin can be read when it comes.
What it leads to. Reform or rebuilding (Ezr 5:13). In 2Ch 29 and Ezr 5, reading the ruin rightly is the first step back.

Part B: Jer 8:19. "Behold, the cry of the daughter of my people …: 'Is the Lord not in Zion? Is her King not in her?' 'Why have they provoked me to anger with their carved images …?'" Then: "The harvest is past, the summer is ended, and we are not saved" (8:20): The people read the ruin as God's absence, as in Deu 31:17. God answers with a counter-question about their provocation; Between them stands the prophet: "My joy is gone; grief is upon me; my heart is sick within me" (8:18); "For the wound of the daughter of my people is my heart wounded; I mourn" (8:21). See §45; Seat . Jer 8:18 "my heart is sick". The prophet's own. Genuine. Jer 8:21 "my heart" is the ESV's; there is no M47 tag in the DB for that verse. It is not counted as a seat.

Part C: Eze 36:18. "I poured out my wrath upon them … I scattered them among the nations." Then: "wherever they came, they profaned my holy name, in that people said of them, 'These are the people of the Lord, and yet they had to go out of his land'" (36:18–20): The nations read the exile as a failure of God. This is the reverse of Deu 29:24–25, where the nations read it rightly; The exiles, simply by being exiles, give the wrong reading.
What it does. "Give to Levi your Thummim … whom you tested at Massah, with whom you quarreled at the waters of Meribah" (Deu 33:8).

How it co-exists. The test is passed by putting God above kin: Levi "said of his father and mother, 'I regard them not'; he disowned his brothers and ignored his children. For they observed your word" (33:9). Contrast U1 §2 (KS), where kinship grounds the refusal of strife.
What it leads to. Teaching and priesthood: "They shall teach Jacob your rules … they shall put incense before you" (33:10).
U1 §12 reads Meribah as human contention with God that costs the leaders the land. Deu 33:8 adds a second reading: at the same place, one party was "godly" and was found faithful by testing.

Part B: Psa 81:7. "In distress you called, and I delivered you; I answered you in the secret place of thunder; I tested you at the waters of Meribah." Then: "O Israel, if you would but listen to me!" (81:8): A second text reads Meribah as God's test (with Deu 33:8). Here the test stands beside a deliverance, and is recalled to call Israel to listen.

What it does: "the people of Israel broke faith in regard to the devoted things, for Achan … took some … And the anger of the Lord burned against the people of Israel" (Jos 7:1). One man took, and the text says the people broke faith; The fear drives a confrontation. The tribes fear the eastern altar: "if you too rebel against the Lord today then tomorrow he will be angry with the whole congregation of Israel" (Jos 22:18). "Did not Achan … break faith … and wrath fell upon all the congregation of Israel? And he did not perish alone for his iniquity" (22:20).
Where it comes from. From memory of shared punishment: "Have we not had enough of the sin at Peor from which even yet we have not cleansed ourselves" (Jos 22:17).

How it co-exists: Accusation and generosity together. The same speech that threatens also offers land: "pass over into the Lord's land … and take for yourselves a possession among us" (Jos 22:19); The accused answer by appealing to God's knowledge: "The Mighty One, God, the Lord! He knows; and let Israel itself know! If it was in rebellion … do not spare us today" (Jos 22:22); The reverse plea. Moses argues against collective anger. David, after the census, asks to bear it alone: "I have sinned … But these sheep, what have they done? Please let your hand be against me and against my father's house". The one who sinned asks that the anger fall on himself only.

What it leads to. The offender removed ("Why did you bring trouble on us? The Lord brings trouble on you today", Jos 7:25), a heap of stones, "Then the Lord turned from his burning anger" (7:26). The misunderstanding over the altar is resolved (22:21–23 onward).

What it does: An oath kept, though obtained by deceit: "We have sworn to them by the Lord … now we may not touch them. This we will do to them: let them live, lest wrath be upon us, because of the oath" (Jos 9:19–20). "Then all the congregation murmured against the leaders" (9:18); A brother warned: judges are to "warn them, that they may not incur guilt before the Lord and wrath may not come upon you and your brothers" (2Ch 19:10). Warning another guards both of them; A foreign king's decree: "Whatever is decreed by the God of heaven, let it be done in full … lest his wrath be against the realm of the king and his sons" (Ezr 7:23). Fear of God's wrath appears in a Persian king.
Where it comes from. From fear of the Lord. "let the fear of the Lord be upon you" (2Ch 19:7); "Thus you shall do in the fear of the Lord, in faithfulness, and with your whole heart" (19:9).
How it co-exists. Against the crowd: in Jos 9 the leaders keep the oath while "all the congregation murmured".
findings.flag: verse taken from the section heading: the claim's references are bare

findings.text: What it leads to. The Gibeonites live as servants (Jos 9:21–23); justice is ordered (2Ch 19); the temple is provided for (Ezr 7).
Seat. None in-verse. Outside: 2Ch 19:9 "with your whole heart". The judges' own. Genuine. Nothing new.

What it does: Given over: "he gave them over to plunderers … so that they could no longer withstand their enemies … And they were in terrible distress" (Judg 2:14–15); Crying out: "when the people of Israel cried out to the Lord, the Lord raised up a deliverer" (Judg 3:9); "We have sinned against you, because we have forsaken our God" (10:10); "do to us whatever seems good to you. Only please deliver us this day" (10:15); Seeking favour: "Jehoahaz sought the favor of the Lord, and the Lord listened to him, for he saw the oppression of Israel" (2Ki 13:4); Relapsing: "whenever the judge died, they turned back and were more corrupt than their fathers … They did not drop any of their practices or their stubborn ways" (Judg 2:19); "Nevertheless, they did not depart from the sins of the house of Jeroboam" (2Ki 13:6).

How it co-exists: God's pity answers the groaning, not a repentance: "the Lord was moved to pity by their groaning because of those who afflicted and oppressed them" (Judg 2:18). In Judg 10:16 they put away the foreign gods, and "he became impatient over the misery of Israel" (the Hebrew has God's nephesh; God's, not the object here); The cry is answered while the relapse is foreseen. Nations are left "to test Israel by them" (Judg 2:22).
What it leads to. Rest "forty years" (Judg 3:11), then again.
Seat. None in-verse. Outside: Judg 3:10 "The Spirit of the Lord was upon him" (Othniel). God's, given. Divine.

Part B: Psa 106:40: "they poured out innocent blood, the blood of their sons and daughters … Then the anger of the Lord was kindled against his people, and he abhorred his heritage; he gave them into the hand of the nations" (106:38–41); The psalm sums the whole cycle: "Many times he delivered them, but they were rebellious in their purposes and were brought low through their iniquity. Nevertheless, he looked upon their distress, when he heard their cry. For their sake he remembered his covenant, and relented" (106:43–45); This confirms the part-A reading that God answers the cry and the distress, not a completed repentance.
What it does. "Because you did not obey the voice of the Lord and did not carry out his fierce wrath against Amalek, therefore the Lord has done this thing to you this day" (1Sa 28:18).
Where it comes from. From disobedience in the commission (1Sa 15, not read here).
findings.flag: verse taken from the section heading: the claim's references are bare

findings.text: How it co-exists. Abandonment, fear and bodily collapse: "God has turned away from me and answers me no more" (1Sa 28:15); "Saul fell at once full length on the ground, filled with fear … And there was no strength in him, for he had eaten nothing all day and all night" (28:20); The medium: "I have taken my life in my hand" (28:21).
What it leads to. Death the next day (28:19).
Seat. None in-verse. Outside: 1Sa 28:21 nephesh. The medium's. Life-sense only.

What it does. "Again the anger of the Lord was kindled against Israel, and he incited David against them, saying, 'Go, number Israel and Judah'" (2Sa 24:1). Joab objects: "why does my lord the king delight in this thing?" (24:3). The king's word prevailed (24:4). Chronicles records that "Joab … began to count, but did not finish. Yet wrath came upon Israel for this" (1Ch 27:24).
Where it comes from. 2Sa 24:1 names God's anger as the source of the incitement. The verse gives no inner cause in David. Joab's question names a delight in the king.

How it co-exists: Conscience afterwards: "David's heart struck him after he had numbered the people … 'I have sinned greatly … I have done very foolishly'" (2Sa 24:10); Choosing whose hand: "Let us fall into the hand of the Lord, for his mercy is great; but let me not fall into the hand of man" (24:14). The one under God's anger chooses God's hand because of God's mercy; Asking to bear it alone.

Seat. None in-verse. Outside: 2Sa 24:10 "David's heart struck him". The bearer's own. Genuine. Read from the M02 side, the struck heart comes after an act that God's anger incited. Pointer for D v2 §3.3.

What it does: Foreseen in Solomon's prayer: "If they sin against you — for there is no one who does not sin — and you are angry with them … yet if they turn their heart … and repent … with all their heart and with all their soul … then hear" (1Ki 8:46–49; 2Ch 6:36–39); Josiah hears the book: "he tore his clothes … 'great is the wrath of the Lord that is kindled against us, because our fathers have not obeyed'" (2Ki 22:11, 13; 2Ch 34:19, 21). The answer names the heart: "because your heart was penitent [tender], and you humbled yourself … and have torn your clothes and wept before me, I also have heard you" (2Ki 22:19; 2Ch 34:27); Rehoboam and the princes: "humbled themselves and said, 'The Lord is righteous.' When the Lord saw that they humbled themselves … I will not destroy them" (2Ch 12:6–7); "when he humbled himself the wrath of the Lord turned from him" (12:12); Hezekiah's pride and humbling: "Hezekiah did not make return according to the benefit done to him, for his heart was proud. Therefore wrath came … But Hezekiah humbled himself for the pride of his heart, both he and the inhabitants of Jerusalem, so that the wrath of the Lord did not come upon them in the days of Hezekiah" (2Ch 32:25–26); Ezra confesses: "you, our God, have punished us less than our iniquities deserved … shall we break your commandments again …? Would you not be angry with us until you consumed us …? … you are just … none can stand before you" (Ezr 9:13–15); Manasseh: "when he was in distress, he entreated the favor of the Lord his God and humbled himself greatly … Then Manasseh knew that the Lord was God" (2Ch 33:12–13).

Where it comes from: From hearing the word (Josiah); From the prophet's announcement (Rehoboam, 2Ch 12:5); From distress (Manasseh; the captives of 1Ki 8); From recognising that one's own heart was proud (Hezekiah). This is the only case in part A where the provocation and the humbling are named in the same heart, in consecutive verses.

How it co-exists: Humbling with a confession of God's justice: "The Lord is righteous" (2Ch 12:6); "you are just" (Ezr 9:15); Humbling with the body: torn clothes and weeping (Josiah); Humbling that is partial. Rehoboam is spared destruction but made to serve Shishak, "that they may know my service and the service of the kingdoms" (2Ch 12:8). Bronze shields replace gold (12:10). And "he did evil, for he did not set his heart to seek the Lord" (12:14). The humbling turned the wrath, and the heart was still not set.

What it leads to: The anger is turned (Rehoboam), deferred past the humbled one's lifetime (Hezekiah; Josiah, "your eyes shall not see all the disaster", 2Ki 22:20), or feared again (Ezra); Josiah's humbling is heard for Josiah, and the wrath on the place stands.

Seat: In the verse: 2Ch 32:25 "his heart was proud" and 32:26 "the pride of his heart". Hezekiah's own. Genuine. A v3 §2.2; D v2 §9.1, §10.1, §11; pilot §2; Outside (all genuine, the bearer's own):; 1Ki 8:47–48 / 2Ch 6:37–38 "turn their heart … with all their heart and with all their soul"; 2Ki 22:19 / 2Ch 34:27 "your heart was penitent / tender"; 2Ch 12:14 "did not set his heart to seek the Lord"; Nothing new in any single seat. What part A adds is a third kind of seat for pilot §2. The pilot has the heart that provokes (the cause) and the spirit that receives (the effect). Part A adds the heart that turns, and so turns the anger away. In these verses, and in §22, it is the human seat most often named in the context of God's anger. For the researcher: whether pilot §2 takes this as a third row.
