What it does: The formula: "the sins of Jeroboam, which he sinned and which he made Israel to sin" (1Ki 14:16; 15:30; 16:13, 26); Each king is measured by the one before: Baasha "walked in the way of Jeroboam" (1Ki 16:2); Omri "did more evil than all who were before him" (16:25); Ahab "did more to provoke the Lord … than all the kings of Israel who were before him" (16:33); Ahaziah walked "in the way of his father and in the way of his mother and in the way of Jeroboam" (22:52–53); Manasseh "led them astray to do more evil than the nations" (2Ki 21:9; 2Ch 33:9).

Where it comes from: Contempt: "you … have cast me behind your back" (1Ki 14:9); Ingratitude for elevation: "Because I exalted you from among the people" (1Ki 14:7); "Since I exalted you out of the dust" (16:2); Self-sale: "you have sold yourself to do what is evil" (1Ki 21:20). "There was none who sold himself … like Ahab, whom Jezebel his wife incited" (21:25); Lightness: "as if it had been a light thing for him to walk in the sins of Jeroboam" (1Ki 16:31); The measure given is David's heart: "you have not been like my servant David, who … followed me with all his heart" (1Ki 14:8).

How it co-exists: The executor is also judged. Baasha is condemned "both because of all the evil that he did … in being like the house of Jeroboam, and also because he destroyed it" (1Ki 16:7). Carrying out the prophesied judgment did not make the executor righteous; One found pleasing in a condemned house. Jeroboam's child "shall come to the grave, because in him there is found something pleasing to the Lord" (1Ki 14:13); Recognition without turning. "Have you found me, O my enemy?" (1Ki 21:20). Ahab recognises the prophet as his enemy.

What it leads to. Whole houses cut off, "as a man burns up dung" (1Ki 14:10). Israel scattered "because of the sins of Jeroboam" (14:15–16). Manasseh's provocation outlives him, and Josiah's reform does not undo it.

Seat. None in-verse. Outside: 1Ki 14:8 "followed me with all his heart". David's own, as the standard. Genuine. Not cited in the batches in this form. Pointer only: the heart appears in these chapters as the measure the kings fail, not as their own seat.

Part C: Zec 10:3. "My anger is hot against the shepherds, and I will punish the leaders." This follows "the household gods utter nonsense … they tell false dreams and give empty consolation. Therefore the people wander like sheep; they are afflicted for lack of a shepherd" (10:2): The leaders' failure leaves the people without a shepherd. Compare §20's kings who "made Israel to sin", and Isa 9:16 in §36.

What it does: "my wrath will be kindled against this place, and it will not be quenched" (2Ki 22:17; 2Ch 34:25); Even after the fullest turning: "Before him there was no king like him, who turned to the Lord with all his heart and with all his soul and with all his might … Still the Lord did not turn from the burning of his great wrath … because of all the provocations with which Manasseh had provoked him" (2Ki 23:25–26); "it came to the point in Jerusalem and Judah that he cast them out from his presence" (2Ki 24:20); "they kept mocking the messengers of God, despising his words and scoffing at his prophets, until the wrath of the Lord rose against his people, until there was no remedy" (2Ch 36:16).

Where it comes from: From accumulated provocation: "since the day their fathers came out of Egypt, even to this day" (2Ki 21:15); From the king's heart hardened against turning: Zedekiah "stiffened his neck and hardened his heart against turning to the Lord" (2Ch 36:13).

How it co-exists: God's compassion is named in the same passage as "no remedy": "The Lord … sent persistently to them by his messengers, because he had compassion on his people" (2Ch 36:15). The persistence of the compassion is what the mocking used up; The one who turns is still heard personally, while the people's end stands. Individual turning and national judgment are held apart here. Contrast Hezekiah, where "he and the inhabitants of Jerusalem" humbled themselves together.
What it leads to. Josiah's death at Megiddo (2Ki 23:29), exile, and the burning of the temple (2Ch 36:17–19).

Seat. None in-verse. Outside: 2Ki 23:25 "all his heart and … all his soul" (Josiah's own). Genuine; 2Ch 36:13 "hardened his heart against turning" (Zedekiah's own). Genuine; 2Ki 22:19 / 2Ch 34:27; Correction. v1 said 2Ki 23:25 was not found in the batch files. It is in E v2 §6 (Torah and obedience). It is not new. Read from the M02 side, it stands as the fullest turning of heart and soul, named next to wrath that did not turn.

Part B: Jer 21:5; 52:3: Jer 52:3 is 2Ki 24:20; "Behold, I will turn back the weapons of war that are in your hands … I myself will fight against you with outstretched hand and strong arm, in anger and in fury and in great wrath" (Jer 21:4–5); "He shall not pity them or spare them" (21:7). God's anger turns the people's own weapons back on them.

What it does: Removal: Josiah "removed all the shrines … which kings of Israel had made, provoking the Lord to anger" (2Ki 23:19); Covenant formed in the heart: "Now it is in my heart to make a covenant with the Lord … in order that his fierce anger may turn away from us. My sons, do not now be negligent" (2Ch 29:10–11); A call to return: "Do not now be stiff-necked as your fathers were, but yield yourselves to the Lord … that his fierce anger may turn away from you. For if you return … your brothers and your children will find compassion" (2Ch 30:8–9); Separation: "Let our officials stand for the whole assembly … until the fierce wrath of our God over this matter is turned away from us" (Ezr 10:14); Sabbath restored: "Now you are bringing more wrath on Israel by profaning the Sabbath" (Neh 13:18), then the gates are shut (13:19); Captives released:; Oded: "you have killed them in a rage that has reached up to heaven … Have you not sins of your own against the Lord your God? … send back the captives … for the fierce wrath of the Lord is upon you" (2Ch 28:9–11); The chiefs: "you propose to bring upon us guilt against the Lord in addition to our present sins … there is fierce wrath against Israel" (28:13); Then: "with the spoil they clothed all who were naked among them … provided them with food and drink, and anointed them, and carrying all the feeble among them on donkeys, they brought them to their kinsfolk" (28:15). Fear of adding to the wrath turns into care for enemies who are also kin; Rebuke acted on: "Should you help the wicked and love those who hate the Lord? Because of this, wrath has gone out against you … Nevertheless, some good is found in you … you … have set your heart to seek God" (2Ch 19:2–3). Jehoshaphat "went out again among the people … and brought them back to the Lord" (19:4).

Where it comes from: From reading the ruin; From a prophet's word (2Ch 19:2; 28:9); From awareness of accumulated guilt ("our guilt is already great", 2Ch 28:13; "we have greatly transgressed", Ezr 10:13); From the fathers' example as a warning ("Did not your fathers act in this way …?", Neh 13:18; "Do not be like your fathers", 2Ch 30:7).

How it co-exists: Mockery. The couriers were "laughed … to scorn and mocked" (2Ch 30:10). "However, some men … humbled themselves and came" (30:11); Opposition within. "Only Jonathan … and Jahzeiah … opposed this" (Ezr 10:15); Practical limits. "the people are many, and it is a time of heavy rain; we cannot stand in the open" (Ezr 10:13).
What it leads to. Passover (2Ki 23:21–22; 2Ch 30), the captives returned (2Ch 28:15), and the Sabbath kept (Neh 13:21). Josiah's reform does not turn the anger for Judah.

Seat: In the verse: 2Ch 29:10 "it is in my heart to make a covenant". Hezekiah's own. Genuine. A v3 §2.2; E v2 §7.1; Outside: 2Ch 19:3 "set your heart to seek God"; The seat of reform is where the intent to turn is formed. This joins §19 (see there).

What it does. "For I was ashamed to ask the king for a band of soldiers … since we had told the king, 'The hand of our God is for good on all who seek him, and the power of his wrath is against all who forsake him'" (Ezr 8:22).

How it co-exists. Fasting and humbling: "I proclaimed a fast … that we might humble ourselves before our God, to seek from him a safe journey" (8:21). "we fasted and implored our God for this, and he listened" (8:23).
What it leads to. A safe journey is sought from God, and "he listened to our entreaty" (8:23).

What it does. "Hear, O our God, for we are despised. Turn back their taunt on their own heads … Do not cover their guilt … for they have provoked you to anger in the presence of the builders" (Neh 4:4–5).
Where it comes from. From being despised. "What are these feeble Jews doing?" (4:2); "if a fox goes up on it he will break down their stone wall!" (4:3).
How it co-exists. The prayer is followed at once by work, not by waiting: "So we built the wall … for the people had a mind to work" (4:6). The enemies' anger then rises again.
What it leads to. The wall "joined together to half its height" (4:6).

Seat. None in-verse. Outside: Neh 4:6 "a mind [heart] to work". Genuine, already read in U1 §17 and §39. What unit 2 adds: in U1 §17 the builders' heart stands between the enemy's two outbursts. It also stands straight after the builders' prayer for God's anger on the mockers. The heart to work follows the handing-over of the enemies to God.

Part B: Psa 56:7; 59:13; 69:24; 79:6; Jer 10:25; 18:23; Lam 3:66 (seven verses). The imprecation is a recurring form in part B, as part A's pointer expected: The grounds given:; enemies who "injure my cause … have waited for my life" (Psa 56:5–6); "the sin of their mouths … the cursing and lies" (59:12); "they persecute him whom you have struck down, and they recount the pain of those you have wounded" (69:26): they add to God's striking; "the nations that do not know you … have devoured Jacob" (79:6–7; Jer 10:25 in the same words); Restraint inside the imprecation: "Kill them not, lest my people forget … consume them in wrath … that they may know that God rules over Jacob" (Psa 59:11, 13). The purpose given is knowledge; Tears and trust beside it: "put my tears in your bottle … This I know, that God is for me" (56:8–9); Paired with the speaker's own plea against anger:; Psa 79:6 is followed by "Do not remember against us our former iniquities" (79:8); Jer 10:25 is preceded by "Correct me, O Lord … not in your anger"; The one who asks for wrath on the nations asks to be corrected without it; The intercessor turned imprecator; "Remember how I stood before you to speak good for them, to turn away your wrath from them" (Jer 18:20); Three verses later: "Forgive not their iniquity … deal with them in the time of your anger" (18:23); The one who turned the anger away now asks for it, because good was repaid with evil: "they have dug a pit for my life" (18:20). See §45; Lam 3:66 comes with "You will give them dullness of heart" (3:65); Seat ; In the verse: none; Outside: Lam 3:65 "dullness of heart". The enemies'. Genuine. Psa 56:6 "my life" (nephesh). Life-sense.

What it does: Eliphaz: "who that was innocent ever perished? … those who plow iniquity and sow trouble reap the same. By the breath of God they perish, and by the blast of his anger they are consumed" (Job 4:7–9); Zophar: "To fill his belly to the full, God will send his burning anger against him and rain it upon him into his body" (20:23); "dragged off in the day of God's wrath. This is the wicked man's portion" (20:28–29); Job contests it from what he has seen: "How often is it that the lamp of the wicked is put out? … That God distributes pains in his anger?" (21:17); "Let their own eyes see their destruction, and let them drink of the wrath" (21:20). He also cites travellers' testimony "that the evil man is spared in the day of calamity, that he is rescued in the day of wrath" (21:29–30); Elihu: "because his anger does not punish … Job opens his mouth in empty talk" (35:15–16); God: "My anger burns against you and against your two friends, for you have not spoken of me what is right, as my servant Job has" (42:7).

Where it comes from. From a rule held with confidence. Eliphaz: "As I have seen" (4:8). His opening is "Is not your fear of God your confidence?" (4:6). The explainers' certainty rests on their own observation, as Job's contest does.

How it co-exists: Job's contest wants God's anger visible on the wicked. "Let him pay it out to them, that they may know it" (21:19). Job does not deny God's anger; he denies that it is seen where the friends say; The wicked in Job 21 reject God outright: "Depart from us! We do not desire the knowledge of your ways" (21:14).

What it leads to: The explainers must go to the sufferer, and he prays for them. "go to my servant Job and offer up a burnt offering for yourselves. And my servant Job shall pray for you, for I will accept his prayer" (42:8). "the Lord restored the fortunes of Job, when he had prayed for his friends" (42:10). The one they explained by God's anger stands between them and God's anger; Job himself has just said: "I had heard of you by the hearing of the ear, but now my eye sees you; therefore I despise myself, and repent in dust and ashes" (42:5–6). God's anger then turns on the friends, not on Job.
Seat: In the verse: Job 4:9 "blast" (ruach). God's breath. Divine; not a human seat. A v3 §2.3 ("anger, breath and nose"); Outside: Job 21:18 "wind" (not inner-being).

What it does: Within: "the arrows of the Almighty are in me; my spirit drinks their poison; the terrors of God are arrayed against me" (Job 6:4); As an enemy: "He has torn me in his wrath and hated me; he has gnashed his teeth at me" (16:9); "He has kindled his wrath against me and counts me as his adversary" (19:11); As a trial with fresh witnesses: "You renew your witnesses against me and increase your vexation toward me" (10:17); As irresistible and unanswerable: "God will not turn back his anger … How then can I answer him …? Though I am in the right, I cannot answer him; I must appeal for mercy to my accuser" (9:13–15). He "removes mountains, and they know it not, when he overturns them in his anger" (9:5).

Where it comes from. The texts give Job no cause. "If I am guilty, woe to me! If I am in the right, I cannot lift up my head" (10:15). "I was at ease, and he broke me apart" (16:12). The reader knows from 42:7 that he spoke rightly; Job, inside the anger, does not.

How it co-exists: Isolation. "He has put my brothers far from me … My relatives have failed me, my close friends have forgotten me" (19:13–14). "Men have gaped at me with their mouth" (16:10); Not being able to see God. "Behold, he passes by me, and I see him not" (9:11). "If I summoned him and he answered me, I would not believe that he was listening to my voice" (9:16); A wish not to have been born. "Why did you bring me out from the womb?" (10:18). "leave me alone, that I may find a little cheer" (10:20); Hope beyond the anger, in the same breath. "Oh that you would hide me in Sheol, that you would conceal me until your wrath be past, that you would appoint me a set time, and remember me! … You would call, and I would answer you; you would long for the work of your hands" (14:13, 15). Job asks for a hiding place from God's anger in God's own keeping, and expects God to long for him afterwards.
What it leads to. Within part A: the sight of God (42:5), repentance "in dust and ashes" (42:6), and God's verdict for him.

Seat: In the verse: Job 6:4 "my spirit drinks their poison". Job's own, as receiver. Genuine. A v3 §1; pilot §2 ("the spirit that receives the anger"); U1 §8 and §39; Outside: Job 6:7 "My appetite refuses to touch them" (nephesh). Appetite-sense, the bearer's own. Job 9:4 "wise in heart" is God's. Job 14:13 is the verse G v3 §16 left for M20 or unit 2. It is read here: its movement is hiding until the wrath passes, followed by being remembered. It is not a death-wish; Nothing new in the seat. Part A has Job 6:4 as its single verse where God's anger is located inside the human seat by the bearer himself. Parts B and C are expected to add the laments.

Part B: Psa 88:7; 88:16; 102:10: Psalm 88, like Job, gives no cause. "Your wrath lies heavy upon me, and you overwhelm me with all your waves" (88:7); "Your wrath has swept over me; your dreadful assaults destroy me" (88:16); "Afflicted and close to death from my youth up" (88:15); Isolation: "You have caused my companions to shun me; you have made me a horror to them" (88:8); "my companions have become darkness" (88:18); Not seeing God: "O Lord, why do you cast my soul away? Why do you hide your face from me?" (88:14); Calling continues: "Every day I call upon you, O Lord; I spread out my hands to you" (88:9); Unlike Job, Psalm 88 has no turn. Its last verse (88:18) ends in darkness; Psa 102:10: "For I eat ashes like bread and mingle tears with my drink, because of your indignation and anger; for you have taken me up and thrown me down" (102:9–10). His enemies "use my name for a curse" (102:8). Then "But you, O Lord, are enthroned forever" (102:12); Seat . Outside: Psa 88:14 "cast my soul away". The bearer's own. Genuine. Pilot §2 (second row) cites Psa 88:7, 16.

What it does. "Then he will speak to them in his wrath, and terrify them in his fury" (Psa 2:5). "Now therefore, O kings, be wise; be warned, O rulers of the earth. Serve the Lord with fear, and rejoice with trembling. Kiss the Son, lest he be angry, and you perish in the way, for his wrath is quickly kindled. Blessed are all who take refuge in him" (2:10–12).
Where it comes from. From rebellion: "Let us burst their bonds apart and cast away their cords from us" (2:3). It is met first with derision: "He who sits in the heavens laughs" (2:4).
How it co-exists: Fear and joy together: "rejoice with trembling"; The refuge is in the one whose wrath is quick. One verse holds the threat and the blessing (2:12).

What it does: "O Lord, rebuke me not in your anger, nor discipline me in your wrath" (Psa 6:1; 38:1 in the same words); "Correct me, O Lord, but in justice; not in your anger, lest you bring me to nothing" (Jer 10:24); The asker does not refuse the correction. He asks for its measure.

Where it comes from: Sin is named in Psalm 38: "there is no health in my bones because of my sin. For my iniquities have gone over my head … My wounds stink and fester because of my foolishness" (38:3–5). Psalm 6 names no sin; Human limits, in Jeremiah: "I know, O Lord, that the way of man is not in himself, that it is not in man who walks to direct his steps" (10:23).

How it co-exists: The body and the soul. "heal me, O Lord, for my bones are troubled. My soul also is greatly troubled. But you, O Lord — how long?" (Psa 6:2–3). "your arrows have sunk into me, and your hand has come down on me. There is no soundness in my flesh because of your indignation" (38:2–3); Two causes for one bodily state. Psa 38:3 names both: "because of your indignation … because of my sin".
What it leads to. A plea for grace (Psa 6:2). In Jeremiah, the next verse asks for wrath on the nations.

Seat: In the verse: Psa 38:3 "flesh" (basar). The bearer's own body, as where the indignation lands. Genuine, bodily; Outside: Psa 6:3 "My soul also is greatly troubled". The bearer's own. Genuine. Not found in the batches, the pilot or unit 1: new as a context seat.

What it does. "Hide not your face from me. Turn not your servant away in anger, O you who have been my help. Cast me not off; forsake me not" (Psa 27:9). "Will the Lord spurn forever …? Has his steadfast love forever ceased? … Has God forgotten to be gracious? Has he in anger shut up his compassion?" (77:7–9).

Where it comes from. In Psalm 27, from a seeker who has already answered God's call: "You have said, 'Seek my face.' My heart says to you, 'Your face, Lord, do I seek'" (27:8). The fear of rejection comes after the heart's own seeking.

How it co-exists: Set against human abandonment: "For my father and my mother have forsaken me, but the Lord will take me in" (27:10); The question is answered by remembering, not by a reply from God: "Then I said, 'I will appeal to this, to the years of the right hand of the Most High.' I will remember the deeds of the Lord" (77:10–11).
What it leads to. "Teach me your way" (27:11); remembering (77:11).
Seat. None in-verse. Outside: Psa 27:8 "My heart says to you". The seeker's own. Genuine.

What it does: "his anger is but for a moment, and his favor is for a lifetime. Weeping may tarry for the night, but joy comes with the morning" (Psa 30:5); "In overflowing anger for a moment I hid my face from you, but with everlasting love I will have compassion on you" (Isa 54:8). "I have sworn that I will not be angry with you" (54:9, "like the days of Noah"); "in my wrath I struck you, but in my favor I have had mercy on you" (60:10); "in a very little while my fury will come to an end" (10:25); "I have no wrath" (27:4); Thanksgiving: "though you were angry with me, your anger turned away, that you might comfort me" (12:1); Gathering after the driving out: "I will gather them from all the countries to which I drove them in my anger … I will give them one heart and one way, that they may fear me forever" (Jer 32:37, 39). "I have hidden my face from this city … Behold, I will bring to it health and healing" (33:5–6).
Where it comes from. Mostly from God's own word. Two human voices testify from inside it: the psalmist (Psa 30) and "you will say in that day" (Isa 12).
findings.flag: verse taken from the section heading: the claim's references are bare

findings.text: How it co-exists: Security broken first: "As for me, I said in my prosperity, 'I shall never be moved.' … you hid your face; I was dismayed" (Psa 30:6–7); Fear removed: "be not afraid of the Assyrians" (Isa 10:24); "I will trust, and will not be afraid" (12:2); Grief addressed: "like a wife deserted and grieved in spirit" (54:6); "O afflicted one, storm-tossed and not comforted" (54:11); Peace offered even to enemies: "let them lay hold of my protection, let them make peace with me" (27:5).
What it leads to: song (Psa 30:4); trust; "With joy you will draw water from the wells of salvation" (Isa 12:3); a new heart given (Jer 32:39).

Seat: In the verse: none; Outside:; Psa 30:3 "you have brought up my soul from Sheol". The speaker's own. Genuine. Not found in the batches: new as a context seat; Isa 54:6 "grieved in spirit". Zion's. Genuine; Jer 32:39 "one heart". Given by God to the people. Genuine.

Part C: Zec 8:14. "As I purposed to bring disaster to you when your fathers provoked me to wrath, and I did not relent … so again have I purposed in these days to bring good to Jerusalem … fear not" (8:14–15): The human response asked for: "Fear not, but let your hands be strong" (8:13); "Speak the truth to one another" (8:16).

What it does: Why? "O God, why do you cast us off forever? Why does your anger smoke against the sheep of your pasture?" (Psa 74:1); How long? "How long, O Lord? Will you be angry forever?" (79:5); "how long will you be angry with your people's prayers?" (80:4); "How long, O Lord? Will you hide yourself forever? How long will your wrath burn like fire?" (89:46); Restore. "you have been angry; oh, restore us" (60:1); "Restore us again, O God of our salvation, and put away your indignation toward us!" (85:4).

Where it comes from. From the ruin, seen and suffered: the taunts of neighbours (79:4; 80:6); the sanctuary destroyed (74:3); the king's crown "in the dust" (89:39); "Our holy and beautiful house … has been burned by fire" (Isa 64:11).

How it co-exists: Past mercy as the ground: "You forgave the iniquity of your people … You withdrew all your wrath … Restore us again" (Psa 85:2–4); "Will you not revive us again, that your people may rejoice in you?" (85:6); Relationship as the ground:; "the sheep of your pasture" (74:1); "Remember your congregation, which you have purchased of old" (74:2); "you are our Father; we are the clay, and you are our potter; we are all the work of your hand … please look, we are all your people" (Isa 64:8–9); Confession, or none; Isa 64 confesses: "you were angry, and we sinned; in our sins we have been a long time, and shall we be saved? … all our righteous deeds are like a polluted garment" (64:5–6); Psa 79 asks: "Do not remember against us our former iniquities" (79:8); Psa 89 does not confess. It holds God to his covenant (89:38–39); The anger reaches even prayer:; "angry with your people's prayers" (Psa 80:4); "There is no one who calls upon your name, who rouses himself to take hold of you; for you have hidden your face from us, and have made us melt in the hand of our iniquities" (Isa 64:7).
Seat. None in-verse. Outside: Psa 89:48 "deliver his soul from the power of Sheol". Life-sense, mortality.
Pointer. Zec 1:12 is an angel's "how long … seventy years?" on behalf of Jerusalem. The laments' question is taken up in heaven, and answered with comfort (1:13).

What it does. "But you, you are to be feared! Who can stand before you when once your anger is roused?" (Psa 76:7). "At his wrath the earth quakes, and the nations cannot endure his indignation" (Jer 10:10).

Where it comes from: From what God has done: "The stouthearted were stripped of their spoil … At your rebuke, O God of Jacob, both rider and horse lay stunned" (Psa 76:5–6); From the living God set against idols: "the instruction of idols is but wood!" (Jer 10:8).

How it co-exists. Awe, and salvation for the humble: "the earth feared and was still, when God arose to establish judgment, to save all the humble of the earth" (Psa 76:8–9). The next verse is U1 §15's Psa 76:10: "Surely the wrath of man shall praise you".
What it leads to. Stillness (76:8).
Seat. None in-verse. Outside: Psa 76:5 "stouthearted". The warriors' heart, stripped. Genuine.

Part C: Nah 1:6; Rev 6:17: "Who can stand before his indignation? Who can endure the heat of his anger?" (Nah 1:6). The next verse: "The Lord is good, a stronghold in the day of trouble; he knows those who take refuge in him" (1:7); "for the great day of their wrath has come, and who can stand?" (Rev 6:17), said by those hiding in the caves; In unit 2 the question comes four times (Psa 76:7; Jer 10:10; Nah 1:6; Rev 6:17), each time by or about those facing the anger; Nahum and Psalm 2 both follow the anger with refuge in the same God.

What it does: "Yet he, being compassionate, atoned for their iniquity and did not destroy them; he restrained his anger often and did not stir up all his wrath" (Psa 78:38); "For my name's sake I defer my anger; for the sake of my praise I restrain it for you, that I may not cut you off" (Isa 48:9); "For I will not contend forever, nor will I always be angry; for the spirit would grow faint before me, and the breath of life that I made" (57:16).

Where it comes from: the reasons: Human frailty: "He remembered that they were but flesh, a wind that passes and comes not again" (Psa 78:39); The human spirit's limit: "the spirit would grow faint before me" (Isa 57:16); God's name: Isa 48:9, 11; Two of the three reasons are about what the human is.

How it co-exists. The human heart has not changed: "Their heart was not steadfast toward him" (Psa 78:37); "they flattered him with their mouths" (78:36); "he went on backsliding in the way of his own heart" (Isa 57:17); "from before birth you were called a rebel" (48:8).

What it leads to: Healing: "I have seen his ways, but I will heal him; I will lead him and restore comfort to him and his mourners" (Isa 57:18); God dwelling with the contrite: "I dwell … with him who is of a contrite and lowly spirit, to revive the spirit of the lowly, and to revive the heart of the contrite" (57:15).

Seat: In the verse:; Isa 57:16 "spirit". The human spirit, as what would faint. Genuine; Isa 57:17 "his own heart". The backslider's. Genuine; Outside: Psa 78:37 "heart"; 78:39 "flesh … wind"; Isa 57:15. Nothing new.

Part C: Eze 20:8; 20:13; 20:21; Hos 11:9: Three times in one chapter: "Then I said I would pour out my wrath upon them … But I acted for the sake of my name" (Eze 20:8–9, 13–14, 21–22: "I withheld my hand"). The chapter ends: "you shall remember your ways … and you shall loathe yourselves … when I deal with you for my name's sake, not according to your evil ways" (20:43–44); Hosea gives another reason: "How can I give you up, O Ephraim? … My heart recoils within me; my compassion grows warm and tender. I will not execute my burning anger … for I am God and not a man" (Hos 11:8–9). The people were "bent on turning away from me" (11:7). They will return "trembling like birds from Egypt" (11:11); The reasons given for restraint now include God's own nature ("God and not a man"), beside human frailty and the name; What the restrained do:; they remember and loathe themselves (Eze 20:43; also 16:63: "that you may remember and be confounded … when I atone for you"); they come trembling (Hos 11:10–11); Seat . Outside: Hos 11:8 "My heart recoils". God's. Divine.

What it does. "For we are brought to an end by your anger; by your wrath we are dismayed" (Psa 90:7). "all our days pass away under your wrath; we bring our years to an end like a sigh" (90:9). "Who considers the power of your anger, and your wrath according to the fear of you?" (90:11).

Where it comes from: Transience before God's eternity: grass that flourishes in the morning and withers by evening (90:5–6); "The years of our life are seventy, or even by reason of strength eighty; yet their span is but toil and trouble; they are soon gone, and we fly away" (90:10); Sin seen: "You have set our iniquities before you, our secret sins in the light of your presence" (90:8).

How it co-exists. Here the wrath is a condition of life, not an event. The response asked for is wisdom: "So teach us to number our days that we may get a heart of wisdom" (90:12). Then: "Return, O Lord! How long? Have pity on your servants!" (90:13).
Seat. None in-verse. Outside: Psa 90:12 "a heart of wisdom". The community's. Genuine. Pilot §2 (second row) already cites 90:7, 9 ("by your wrath we are dismayed").
What it adds. Psa 90:11–12 makes considering the anger the way to a wise heart.

What it does: "Riches do not profit in the day of wrath, but righteousness delivers from death" (Pro 11:4); "The mouth of forbidden women is a deep pit; he with whom the Lord is angry will fall into it" (22:14); "Do not rejoice when your enemy falls, and let not your heart be glad when he stumbles, lest the Lord see it and be displeased, and turn away his anger from him" (24:17–18); "Let not your mouth lead you into sin, and do not say before the messenger that it was a mistake. Why should God be angry at your voice and destroy the work of your hands?" (Ecc 5:6).

How it co-exists: The anger works through the person's own folly: the one under anger falls into the pit (Pro 22:14); Gloating redirects the anger, away from the enemy (24:18); Fear: "God is the one you must fear" (Ecc 5:7).

Seat: In the verse: Ecc 5:6 "lead" (basar): literally "let not your mouth cause your flesh to sin". The speaker's flesh, as the self that sins. Genuine; Outside:; Pro 24:17 "let not your heart be glad". Genuine; Pro 22:15 "Folly is bound up in the heart of a child".

What it does: The refrain, five times: "For all this his anger has not turned away, and his hand is stretched out still" (Isa 5:25; 9:12, 17, 21; 10:4); "The people did not turn to him who struck them, nor inquire of the Lord of hosts" (9:13); "it set him on fire all around, but he did not understand; it burned him up, but he did not take it to heart" (42:25); "The whole land is made desolate, but no man lays it to heart" (Jer 12:11).

Where it comes from: Pride: "The bricks have fallen, but we will build with dressed stones" (Isa 9:10); Leaders who mislead: "those who guide this people have been leading them astray" (9:16); Rejecting the law: "they have rejected the law of the Lord of hosts" (5:24).

How it co-exists: The people consume themselves: "no one spares another. They slice meat on the right, but are still hungry … each devours the flesh of his own arm, Manasseh devours Ephraim, and Ephraim devours Manasseh" (Isa 9:19–21); Futility: "They have sown wheat and have reaped thorns; they have tired themselves out but profit nothing" (Jer 12:13); Wealth is no refuge: "What will you do on the day of punishment …? To whom will you flee for help, and where will you leave your wealth?".
What it leads to. The hand stays stretched out. Isa 42 asks the hearers: "Who among you will give ear to this, will attend and listen for the time to come?" (42:23).

Seat: In the verse: Isa 42:25 "he did not take it to heart". The people's own heart, as where the meaning of the blow should be received, and is not. Genuine; Outside: Jer 12:11 "no man lays it to heart". Isa 9:20 "flesh of his own arm" (bodily, figurative).

Part C: Zep 3:8; Zec 7:12; Mal 1:4: Correction refused: "I said, 'Surely you will fear me; you will accept correction' … But all the more they were eager to make all their deeds corrupt" (Zep 3:7). The next verse (3:8) is wrath on the nations, followed by "a pure speech, that all of them may call upon the name of the Lord" (3:9); The heart made hard against hearing: "they refused to pay attention and turned a stubborn shoulder and stopped their ears … They made their hearts diamond-hard lest they should hear the law … Therefore great anger came" (Zec 7:11–12); Refusal returned in kind: "As I called, and they would not hear, so they called, and I would not hear" (7:13); Rebuilding against the blow, again: "If Edom says, 'We are shattered but we will rebuild the ruins,' the Lord of hosts says, 'They may build, but I will tear down … the people with whom the Lord is angry forever'" (Mal 1:4). This is Isa 9:10's "we will build with dressed stones" said by another nation; Seat . In the verse: Zec 7:12 "hearts diamond-hard". The people's own. Genuine. The same verse has "his Spirit" (God's; divine). Outside: Zec 7:10 "devise evil against another in your heart"; What part C adds. Part B's "heart that does not take it in" was a failure to understand. Zec 7:12 names an act: the heart made hard so as not to hear.

What it does: "Woe to Assyria, the rod of my anger; the staff in their hands is my fury! Against a godless nation I send him" (Isa 10:5–6); "I myself have commanded my consecrated ones, and have summoned my mighty men to execute my anger, my proudly exulting ones" (13:3); "the weapons of his indignation" (13:5; Jer 50:25).

Where it comes from: the agent's own heart: Assyria: "But he does not so intend, and his heart does not so think; but it is in his heart to destroy, and to cut off nations not a few; for he says: 'Are not my commanders all kings?'" (Isa 10:7–8); Babylon: "I was angry with my people … I gave them into your hand; you showed them no mercy; on the aged you made your yoke exceedingly heavy. You said, 'I shall be mistress forever,' so that you did not lay these things to heart or remember their end" (47:6–7). And "who say in your heart, 'I am, and there is no one besides me'" (47:8).
How it co-exists: Pride: "proudly exulting" (13:3); "the arrogant heart of the king of Assyria" (10:12); Excess beyond the commission: "you showed them no mercy" (47:6).

What it leads to. The agent is judged in turn: "he will punish the speech of the arrogant heart of the king of Assyria" (Isa 10:12); Babylon: "I set a snare for you and you were taken, O Babylon, and you did not know it … because you opposed the Lord" (Jer 50:24).

Seat. None in-verse. Outside: Isa 10:7 "heart" ×2; Isa 10:12; Isa 47:8; Isa 47:7 "did not lay these things to heart" was not found in the batches: new as a context seat. Babylon's heart, like Israel's in §36, does not take in what it is doing.

Revisit of part A §17 and §20: Saul failed to carry out the wrath. Here the agents carry it out beyond what was meant. Both are judged; Part A §20 found Baasha condemned "also because he destroyed" Jeroboam's house (1Ki 16:7). §37 shows the same pattern with nations as the agents.

Part C: Zec 1:15. "I am exceedingly angry with the nations that are at ease; for while I was angry but a little, they furthered the disaster." The agents went beyond the measure, as in Isa 47:6. Part C also has aligned agents; they are read separately in §53.

What it does: "Behold, the day of the Lord comes, cruel, with wrath and fierce anger" (Isa 13:9); "the Lord is enraged against all the nations" (34:2); "the peaceful folds are devastated because of the fierce anger of the Lord" (Jer 25:37); The human side:; "Therefore all hands will be feeble, and every human heart will melt. They will be dismayed: pangs and agony will seize them … They will look aghast at one another; their faces will be aflame" (Isa 13:7–8); "like a hunted gazelle, or like sheep with none to gather them, each will turn to his own people, and each will flee to his own land" (13:14); "No refuge will remain for the shepherds … the cry of the shepherds, and the wail of the lords of the flock!" (Jer 25:35–36); "I will terrify Elam before their enemies and before those who seek their life" (49:37); Onlookers: "everyone who passes by Babylon shall be appalled, and hiss because of all her wounds" (50:13).

Where it comes from: Pride: "I will put an end to the pomp of the arrogant, and lay low the pompous pride of the ruthless" (Isa 13:11); Exulting over plunder: "Though you rejoice, though you exult, O plunderers of my heritage" (Jer 50:11).
How it co-exists: Summons to hear: "Draw near, O nations, to hear" (Isa 34:1); Restoration named for a foreign nation: "But in the latter days I will restore the fortunes of Elam" (Jer 49:39).
Seat: In the verse: Jer 49:37 "life". Elam's. Life-sense; Outside: Isa 13:7 "every human heart will melt". Genuine. Not found in the batches: new as a context seat.

Part C: Eze 7:12; 7:14; 7:19; 21:17; 21:31; 30:15; 38:18; 38:19; Mic 5:15; Zep 1:15; 1:18; Luk 21:23: Ordinary life suspended: "Let not the buyer rejoice, nor the seller mourn, for wrath is upon all their multitude" (Eze 7:12); Paralysis: "They have blown the trumpet and made everything ready, but none goes to battle" (7:14); The body: "All hands are feeble, and all knees turn to water. They put on sackcloth, and horror covers them. Shame is on all faces" (7:17–18); Survivors "moaning, each one over his iniquity" (7:16); Wealth useless: "Their silver and gold are not able to deliver them in the day of the wrath of the Lord. They cannot satisfy their hunger … For it was the stumbling block of their iniquity" (7:19); "Neither their silver nor their gold shall be able to deliver them on the day of the wrath of the Lord" (Zep 1:18). The wisdom saying of Pro 11:4 appears in prophecy twice; Blindness: "I will bring distress on mankind, so that they shall walk like the blind" (Zep 1:17); "the mighty man cries aloud there" (1:14); Hearts melting: "that their hearts may melt" (Eze 21:15); Every man against his brother: "Every man's sword will be against his brother" (Eze 38:21), as in Isa 9:19–21; In the Gospel: "Alas for women who are pregnant and for those who are nursing infants in those days! For there will be great distress upon the earth and wrath against this people" (Luk 21:23), with "let those who are in Judea flee to the mountains" (21:21); Seat ; In the verse: Eze 7:19 "hunger" (nephesh). The people's appetite. Appetite-sense; Outside: Eze 21:15 "that their hearts may melt". Genuine. Not found in the batches: new as a context seat.

What it does. "Come, my people, enter your chambers, and shut your doors behind you; hide yourselves for a little while until the fury has passed by" (Isa 26:20). "Go out of the midst of her, my people! Let every one save his life from the fierce anger of the Lord!" (Jer 51:45).
Where it comes from. From God's own call. The anger is on others (Isa 26:21; Babylon).
How it co-exists: Fear addressed: "Let not your heart faint, and be not fearful at the report heard in the land" (Jer 51:46); Hope: "Your dead shall live; their bodies shall rise" (Isa 26:19).
Job asked for this. "Oh that you would hide me in Sheol, that you would conceal me until your wrath be past". In Isa 26:20, God offers his people what Job asked for. Revisit note for §26.
Seat: In the verse: Jer 51:45 "life". The people's own. Life-sense; Outside: Jer 51:46 "Let not your heart faint". Genuine.

Part C: Zep 2:2; 2:3; Rev 6:16: Hiding offered, with "perhaps": "Gather together, yes, gather, O shameless nation, before the decree takes effect … Seek the Lord, all you humble of the land … seek righteousness; seek humility; perhaps you may be hidden on the day of the anger of the Lord" (Zep 2:1–3). The way to be hidden is seeking, humility and righteousness, and even then only "perhaps"; Hiding from God, not in him: "the kings of the earth and the great ones … and everyone, slave and free, hid themselves in the caves and among the rocks of the mountains, calling to the mountains and rocks, 'Fall on us and hide us from the face of him who is seated on the throne, and from the wrath of the Lamb'" (Rev 6:15–16); This is the reverse of Isa 26:20. There God calls his people into their chambers. Here people ask the mountains to hide them from God.

What it does: "you who have drunk from the hand of the Lord the cup of his wrath, who have drunk to the dregs the bowl, the cup of staggering" (Isa 51:17); "Your sons have fainted; they lie at the head of every street like an antelope in a net; they are full of the wrath of the Lord" (51:20); The prophet as cup-bearer (B3): "Take from my hand this cup of the wine of wrath, and make all the nations to whom I send you drink it. They shall drink and stagger and be crazed" (Jer 25:15–16). "So I took the cup from the Lord's hand" (25:17); "You must drink!" (25:28).

How it co-exists: No one left to help: "There is none to guide her among all the sons she has borne" (Isa 51:18); "who will console you? … who will comfort you?" (51:19); "drunk, but not with wine" (51:21); Humiliation: "you have made your back like the ground and like the street for them to pass over" (51:23); The community lament uses the same image: "you have given us wine to drink that made us stagger".

What it leads to. The cup is taken away and given to the tormentors: "Behold, I have taken from your hand the cup of staggering; the bowl of my wrath you shall drink no more; and I will put it into the hand of your tormentors" (Isa 51:22–23). It is done by "your God who pleads the cause of his people" (51:22).
Seat. None in-verse. Outside: Isa 51:23 "to you" (nephesh). Zion's self. Self-sense. Not found in the batches.

Revisit of U1 §34 and its pointer. U1 §34 is "anger and passion as a drink given to others" (Hab 2:15; Rev 14:8; 18:3). Its pointer was "the cup that comes round" (Hab 2:16; Rev 14:10): Isa 51:22–23 is the cup coming round: taken from the one who drank and given to the tormentors; Part C (Hab 2:16; Rev 14:10) will be read against it.

Part C: Rev 14:10; 16:19: "Fallen, fallen is Babylon the great, she who made all nations drink the wine of the passion of her sexual immorality". Then: "he also will drink the wine of God's wrath, poured full strength into the cup of his anger" (14:10). And: "God remembered Babylon the great, to make her drain the cup of the wine of the fury of his wrath" (16:19); Context read for the U1 §34 pointer: "Woe to him who makes his neighbors drink — you pour out your wrath and make them drunk … Drink, yourself … The cup in the Lord's right hand will come around to you" (Hab 2:15–16); "The cup that comes round" now has three texts:; Isa 51:22–23: taken from Zion, given to the tormentors; Hab 2:16: the one who made others drink must drink; Rev 14:8–10 and 16:19: Babylon made the nations drink, and drains God's cup; The human side is the maker of drink who becomes the drinker. "Here is a call for the endurance of the saints" (Rev 14:12); Under the cup, cursing, not repenting: "they cursed God for the plague of the hail" (16:21); "They did not repent and give him glory" (16:9; also 16:11). Compare §36.

What it does: "He saw that there was no man, and wondered that there was no one to intercede; then his own arm brought him salvation" (Isa 59:16); "wrath to his adversaries" (59:18); "I have trodden the winepress alone, and from the peoples no one was with me" (63:3); "I looked, but there was no one to help; I was appalled, but there was no one to uphold; so my own arm brought me salvation, and my wrath upheld me" (63:5).

Where it comes from. The human side here is an absence: Part A §4 had Moses standing before the anger, and Psa 106:23 says "had not Moses … stood in the breach"; Isa 64:7 gives the people's side of the same absence: "There is no one who calls upon your name, who rouses himself to take hold of you".

How it co-exists. Redemption: "a Redeemer will come to Zion, to those in Jacob who turn from transgression" (59:20); "my year of redemption had come" (63:4); "Surely they are my people … And he became their Savior" (63:8).
Seat. None in-verse. Outside: Isa 63:4 "in my heart". God's. Divine.
#1892 pointer Isa 59:1–2 ("sins that separate"). It is not an M02 verse and is outside ±2 of 59:18. Not read here, so the pointer stays open.

Part C: Eze 14:19; 22:24; 22:31: "I found none": "And I sought for a man among them who should build up the wall and stand in the breach before me for the land, that I should not destroy it, but I found none. Therefore I have poured out my indignation upon them" (Eze 22:30–31, context read); Ezekiel uses the image of Psa 106:23, to say that no one did; Before it, every group is named as having failed: prophets (22:25, 28), priests (22:26), princes (22:27), the people of the land (22:29); Even the righteous could not stand for others: "even if Noah, Daniel, and Job were in it … they would deliver neither son nor daughter. They would deliver but their own lives by their righteousness" (14:20); Part A §4 had intercession that succeeded. Part C has intercession sought and not found (22:30), refused (9:8–10), and declared insufficient (14:20); Seat . Outside: Eze 14:20 "their own lives" (nephesh). Life-sense. Eze 22:25 "devoured human lives".

What it does: "you say, 'I am innocent; surely his anger has turned from me.' Behold, I will bring you to judgment for saying, 'I have not sinned'" (Jer 2:35). This is said to a people with "the lifeblood of the guiltless poor" on their skirts (2:34); The prophets "say continually to those who despise the word of the Lord, 'It shall be well with you'; and to everyone who stubbornly follows his own heart, they say, 'No disaster shall come upon you'" (23:17). The answer: "Behold, the storm of the Lord! Wrath has gone forth" (23:19).
Where it comes from: Innocence declared of oneself; Prophets who were not sent: "who among them has stood in the council of the Lord …?" (23:18).

How it co-exists: Jeremiah's own cry: "Ah, Lord God, surely you have utterly deceived this people and Jerusalem, saying, 'It shall be well with you,' whereas the sword has reached their very life" (4:10); The city's confidence: "Who shall come down against us?" (21:13).
Seat. None in-verse. Outside: Jer 23:17 "stubbornly follows his own heart".

Revisit of part A §7. Deu 29:19 has one man blessing himself: "I shall be safe, though I walk in the stubbornness of my heart". Jeremiah shows the same false peace spoken by prophets to a whole people, in almost the same words ("stubbornly follows his own heart"). F v4 §9.6 ("Peace — true and false") already holds both.

Part C: Eze 13:13; 13:15: The whitewashed wall: "When the wall falls, will it not be said to you, 'Where is the coating …?'" (13:12). "the prophets of Israel who … saw visions of peace for her, when there was no peace" (13:16), and the daughters "who prophesy out of their own hearts" (13:17); False peace is a wall coated over, and the wrath is what shows what the coating hid; Seat ; In the verse: Eze 13:13 "wind". Spurious; Outside: Eze 13:17 "out of their own hearts". The false prophetesses'. Genuine.

What it does: "Return, faithless Israel, declares the Lord. I will not look on you in anger, for I am merciful … I will not be angry forever. Only acknowledge your guilt" (Jer 3:12–13); "Circumcise yourselves to the Lord; remove the foreskin of your hearts … lest my wrath go forth like fire" (4:4); "Execute justice in the morning, and deliver from the hand of the oppressor him who has been robbed, lest my wrath go forth like fire" (21:12); "It may be that their plea for mercy will come before the Lord, and that every one will turn from his evil way, for great is the anger and wrath that the Lord has pronounced against this people" (36:7).

How it co-exists: Pretense warned against: Judah "did not return to me with her whole heart, but in pretense" (3:10); Fasting: the scroll is read "on a day of fasting" (36:6), and the people "proclaimed a fast before the Lord" (36:9).
Seat: In the verse: Jer 4:4 "foreskin of your hearts". The hearers' own heart, as what must be opened. Genuine; Outside: Jer 3:10 "whole heart … pretense".

What it adds. Part A §22 had reformers acting to turn the anger away. Here God calls to the heart itself: the heart is named as the place of the change required (4:4), and pretense in the heart as what fails (3:10).

Part C: Hos 14:4; Zec 1:2: Hosea gives the words to say: "Take with you words and return to the Lord; say to him, 'Take away all iniquity … Assyria shall not save us; we will not ride on horses; and we will say no more, "Our God," to the work of our hands. In you the orphan finds mercy.'" (Hos 14:2–3). The answer: "I will heal their apostasy; I will love them freely, for my anger has turned from them" (14:4); "The Lord was very angry with your fathers … Return to me, says the Lord of hosts, and I will return to you … Do not be like your fathers" (Zec 1:2–4); What part C adds. In Hos 14:2–3 God gives the returning people the words to say, and the answer is that his anger has turned. The words renounce three false refuges: Assyria, horses, and idols. Jer 3:13 ("Only acknowledge your guilt") gave what to acknowledge. Hosea gives the whole speech.

What it does: "For this put on sackcloth, lament and wail, for the fierce anger of the Lord has not turned back from us" (Jer 4:8); "Cut off your hair and cast it away; raise a lamentation on the bare heights, for the Lord has rejected and forsaken the generation of his wrath" (7:29); The land itself: "I looked, and behold, there was no man … the fruitful land was a desert … before his fierce anger" (4:25–26); "For this the earth shall mourn" (4:28).
Where it comes from. From the anger not turned, and from a people that "did not accept discipline; truth has perished" (7:28).

How it co-exists: Courage fails: "In that day … courage shall fail both king and officials. The priests shall be appalled and the prophets astounded" (4:9); A limit: "yet I will not make a full end" (4:27).
Seat. None in-verse. Outside: Jer 4:9 "courage [heart] shall fail both king and officials" (both are lev). The leaders' own. Genuine.
Pointer. In part A §6, Aaron's sons were forbidden to mourn, "lest … wrath come" (Lev 10:6). Here mourning is commanded because the wrath has come.

Part C: Eze 19:12. "And you, take up a lamentation for the princes of Israel" (19:1, context read). "But the vine was plucked up in fury … This is a lamentation and has become a lamentation" (19:12, 14). Also Eze 6:11: "Clap your hands and stamp your foot and say, Alas". The lament is commanded of the prophet himself: Seat . Eze 19:12 "east wind". Spurious.

What it does: "In your forbearance take me not away; know that for your sake I bear reproach" (Jer 15:15); "Your words were found, and I ate them, and your words became to me a joy and the delight of my heart … I sat alone, because your hand was upon me, for you had filled me with indignation" (15:16–17); "Remember how I stood before you to speak good for them, to turn away your wrath from them" (18:20). The same verse: "they have dug a pit for my life".
Where it comes from. From the word eaten (15:16) and the commission.
How it co-exists: Grief for the people under the anger: "My joy is gone; grief is upon me; my heart is sick within me"; Isolation: "I sat alone" (15:17); Imprecation after rejection: 18:23.
What it leads to. In Jer 18, the turn from intercession to imprecation.
findings.flag: verse taken from the section heading: the claim's references are bare

findings.text: Seat: In the verse: Jer 18:20 "life". The prophet's. Life-sense; Outside:; Jer 15:16 "delight of my heart"; Jer 8:18 "my heart is sick".

Revisit of U1 §15 and pilot §2.3. The pilot calls Jer 6:11 and 15:17 "the one place in M02 where divine anger becomes a human inner operation", and U1 §15 adds Eze 3:14: Part B adds what the vessel costs the prophet from the people: reproach (15:15) and a pit dug for him (18:20); The pilot's statement about the anger inside the prophet stands.

What it does. "The anger of the Lord will not turn back until he has executed and accomplished the intents of his heart. In the latter days you will understand it clearly" (Jer 23:20). "Behold the storm of the Lord! Wrath has gone forth" (30:23), and "The fierce anger of the Lord will not turn back until he has executed and accomplished the intentions of his mind. In the latter days you will understand this" (30:24).

How it co-exists: In Jer 23, set against false prophets: "if they had stood in my council, then they would have proclaimed my words to my people, and they would have turned them from their evil way" (23:22); In Jer 30, set after restoration: "you shall be my people, and I will be your God" (30:22). A prince draws near: "for who would dare of himself to approach me?" (30:21).

Seat: In the verse: Jer 23:20 "heart" and 30:24 "mind". God's. Divine; Outside: Jer 30:21 "of himself" (lev, "who would pledge his heart"). The prince's own. Genuine. Not found in the batches: new as a context seat.

What it does: "As my anger and my wrath were poured out on the inhabitants of Jerusalem, so my wrath will be poured out on you when you go to Egypt" (Jer 42:18); In Egypt: "Why do you provoke me to anger with the works of your hands, making offerings to other gods in the land of Egypt where you have come to live …?" (44:8).

Where it comes from: Fear: "the sword that you fear shall overtake you there … the famine of which you are afraid shall follow close after you" (42:16); Asking and not doing: "For you sent me to the Lord your God, saying, 'Pray for us … whatever the Lord our God says, declare to us and we will do it.' And I have this day declared it to you, but you have not obeyed" (42:20–21); Forgetting: "Have you forgotten the evil of your fathers …?" (44:9); No humbling: "They have not humbled themselves even to this day, nor have they feared" (44:10).

How it co-exists: They saw the ruin: "You have seen all the disaster that I brought upon Jerusalem" (44:2). They repeated its cause; Self-harm: "Why do you commit this great evil against yourselves …?" (44:7).
What it leads to. "You shall become an execration … You shall see this place no more" (42:18); "cut off … a curse and a taunt among all the nations" (44:8).
Seat. None in-verse. Outside: Jer 42:20 "at the cost of your lives" (nephesh). Life-sense. Not found in the batches; Jer 44:7 "against yourselves" (nephesh). Genuine, the self harmed.

What it adds: Flight commanded set against flight forbidden here (42:19). Fear of the sword drives them into the wrath; Part A §12 said that reading the ruin rightly was the first step back (2Ch 29; Ezr 5). Jer 44 is the counter-case: they saw the ruin (44:2) and did not turn.

What it does: "Is it nothing to you, all you who pass by? Look and see if there is any sorrow like my sorrow, which was brought upon me, which the Lord inflicted on the day of his fierce anger" (Lam 1:12); "The Lord has become like an enemy" (2:5). "He has bent his bow like an enemy … and he has killed all who were delightful in our eyes" (2:4). "The Lord has made Zion forget festival and Sabbath" (2:6); "you have killed them in the day of your anger, slaughtering without pity" (2:21); "on the day of the anger of the Lord no one escaped or survived" (2:22); "I am the man who has seen affliction under the rod of his wrath" (3:1); "You have wrapped yourself with anger and pursued us, killing without pity; you have wrapped yourself with a cloud so that no prayer can pass through" (3:43–44); "The Lord gave full vent to his wrath" (4:11).

Where it comes from. Sin is confessed: "My transgressions were bound into a yoke" (1:14); "We have transgressed and rebelled, and you have not forgiven" (3:42); "for the sins of her prophets and the iniquities of her priests" (4:13).

How it co-exists: The body of the one speaking: "From on high he sent fire; into my bones he made it descend … he has left me stunned, faint all the day long" (1:13); "He has made my flesh and my skin waste away; he has broken my bones" (3:4); "He has walled me about so that I cannot escape; he has made my chains heavy; though I call and cry for help, he shuts out my prayer" (3:7–8); Hunger at its worst: "The hands of compassionate women have boiled their own children" (4:10); "Should women eat the fruit of their womb …?" (2:20); Pouring out the heart: "Arise, cry out in the night … Pour out your heart like water before the presence of the Lord! Lift your hands to him for the lives of your children" (2:19); "Let us lift up our hearts and hands to God in heaven" (3:41); Hope inside the lament (context of Lam 3:1, read this session):; "My soul continually remembers it and is bowed down within me. But this I call to mind, and therefore I have hope: The steadfast love of the Lord never ceases" (3:20–22); "For the Lord will not cast off forever, for, though he cause grief, he will have compassion … for he does not afflict from his heart or grieve the children of men" (3:31–33); "Let us test and examine our ways, and return to the Lord!" (3:40); Outsiders' disbelief: "The kings of the earth did not believe … that foe or enemy could enter the gates of Jerusalem" (4:12).

What it leads to. "Restore us to yourself, O Lord, that we may be restored! Renew our days as of old — unless you have utterly rejected us, and you remain exceedingly angry with us" (5:21–22). The book ends on the question.

Seat: In the verse: none; Outside:; Lam 2:19 "pour out your heart like water"; 3:20 "My soul … is bowed down"; 3:41 "lift up our hearts"; 3:33 "from his heart": God's, divine; Lam 1:11 "revive their strength" (nephesh): appetite/life-sense, not found in the batches.

#1892 pointer: Lam 3:7 against 3:33. Both were read here in context: The same speaker holds both: the experience of being walled in and chained (3:7), and the confession that God "does not afflict from his heart" (3:33); The #1892 first pass already set the two side by side. What part B adds is that Lam 3:1, an M02 verse, puts the whole chapter under "the rod of his wrath". No change to #1892.
Data note. Lam 3:2 has no verse row in `iba.db`. This is by design (`governance.verse_gap_by_design`), and the reading went on to 3:3.
findings.flag: verse taken from the section heading: the claim's references are bare

findings.text: Compared with §31. The community laments in Psalms ask "how long?". Lamentations speaks after the day itself, and adds confession, the body, and the unfinished question (5:22).

What it does: "Thus shall my anger spend itself, and I will vent my fury upon them and satisfy myself. And they shall know that I am the Lord — that I have spoken in my jealousy" (Eze 5:13); "Then you will know that I am the Lord, who strikes" (7:9); For the nations too: "Then they will know that I am the Lord, when I lay my vengeance upon them" (25:17), the Philistines having "acted revengefully and took vengeance with malice of soul" (25:15); As a sign to others: "You shall be a reproach and a taunt, a warning and a horror, to the nations all around you" (5:15).
Where it comes from. From the anger carried through to its end: "the end is upon you … I will judge you according to your ways" (7:3); "My eye will not spare, and I will have no pity" (5:11; 7:4, 9).

How it co-exists: The prophet's gesture: "Clap your hands and stamp your foot and say, Alas" (6:11); No refuge by distance or survival: "He who is far off shall die of pestilence, and he who is near shall fall by the sword, and he who is left and is preserved shall die of famine" (6:12); Pride named: "the rod has blossomed; pride has budded" (7:10).
What it leads to. Knowledge that comes through judgment, not before it. In Eze 20:43–44 the same knowledge comes with remembering and self-loathing.
Seat. None in-verse. Outside: Eze 25:15 "malice of soul" (nephesh). The Philistines'. Genuine.

Linked to earlier sections: Part B §24: "that they may know that God rules" (Psa 59:13); Part B §46: "In the latter days you will understand" (Jer 23:20); Across the unit, God's anger is said to be for knowledge: of his rule (Psalms), of his purpose later (Jeremiah), of his name now (Ezekiel).

What it does: "You also played the whore with the Egyptians, your lustful neighbors, multiplying your whoring, to provoke me to anger" (Eze 16:26); "I will judge you as women who commit adultery and shed blood are judged, and bring upon you the blood of wrath and jealousy" (16:38); Carried out by others (B3): "I will direct my jealousy against you, that they may deal with you in fury" (23:25).

Where it comes from: Never satisfied: "you played the whore also with the Assyrians, because you were not satisfied; yes, you played the whore with them, and still you were not satisfied" (16:28); Forgetting: "you have not remembered the days of your youth" (16:43); The blood of children: "because of the blood of your children that you gave to them" (16:36).
How it co-exists: Shame, from a surprising source: the Philistines "were ashamed of your lewd behavior" (16:27); Handed on: "Like mother, like daughter" (16:44).

What it leads to: The anger ends in calm: "So will I satisfy my wrath on you, and my jealousy shall depart from you. I will be calm and will no more be angry" (16:42); "I will put an end to your lewdness … so that you shall not lift up your eyes to them or remember Egypt anymore" (23:27); The chapter's end (context read): "that you may remember and be confounded, and never open your mouth again because of your shame, when I atone for you" (16:63).
Seat: In the verse: Eze 16:26 "lustful" (basar). The Egyptians' flesh, in a sexual sense. Bodily; Outside: Eze 16:27 "the greed of your enemies" (nephesh). Appetite-sense. Not found in the batches.

What it does: "What is in your mind shall never happen — the thought, 'Let us be like the nations, like the tribes of the countries, and worship wood and stone.' As I live … surely with a mighty hand and an outstretched arm and with wrath poured out I will be king over you" (Eze 20:32–33); "I will bring you out from the peoples and gather you … with wrath poured out. And I will bring you into the wilderness of the peoples, and there I will enter into judgment with you face to face" (20:34–35); "Where now is your king, to save you …? Where are all your rulers — those of whom you said, 'Give me a king and princes'? I gave you a king in my anger, and I took him away in my wrath" (Hos 13:10–11).
Where it comes from: The wish in the mind (Eze 20:32); The request for a king (Hos 13:10); Refusal to be inquired of: "I will not be inquired of by you" (Eze 20:31).
How it co-exists. Wrath and gathering in one act. "with wrath poured out" is said of the gathering itself (20:34), not only of the scattering.
What it leads to. Judgment "face to face" (20:35), and remembering (20:43).
Seat. None in-verse. Outside: Eze 20:32 "What is in your mind" (ruach). The people's. Genuine.

What it adds. What the people asked for (a king; to be like the nations) is answered in anger: by being given it (Hosea) and by being refused it (Ezekiel). Compare Psa 78's craving granted with anger.
findings.flag: verse taken from the section heading: the claim's references are bare

findings.text: What it does: "the house of Israel has become dross to me … As one gathers silver and bronze and iron and lead and tin into a furnace, to blow the fire on it in order to melt it, so I will gather you in my anger and in my wrath, and I will put you in and melt you" (Eze 22:18, 20); "you shall know that I am the Lord; I have poured out my wrath upon you" (22:22); The pot: "Woe to the bloody city, to the pot whose corrosion is in it, and whose corrosion has not gone out of it!" (24:6). "To rouse my wrath, to take vengeance, I have set on the bare rock the blood she has shed, that it may not be covered" (24:8).

Where it comes from: Refused cleansing: "because I would have cleansed you and you were not cleansed from your uncleanness, you shall not be cleansed anymore till I have satisfied my fury upon you" (24:13); Effort without change: "She has wearied herself with toil; its abundant corrosion does not go out of it" (24:12); Blood left uncovered (24:7).
How it co-exists. "I will not go back; I will not spare; I will not relent" (24:14).
What it leads to. Melting (22:22), and cleansing by fire only after the offer of cleansing was refused.
Seat. None in-verse. Outside: Eze 24:10 "meat" (basar). Spurious.
Compared with part B. Isa 48:10 has "I have tried you in the furnace of affliction" with restraint. In Ezekiel the furnace is not refining but melting, because the cleansing was refused.

What it does: "I will lay my vengeance upon Edom by the hand of my people Israel, and they shall do in Edom according to my anger and according to my wrath" (Eze 25:14). Edom had "acted revengefully against the house of Judah" (25:12); "he is God's servant for your good. But if you do wrong, be afraid, for he does not bear the sword in vain. For he is the servant of God, an avenger who carries out God's wrath on the wrongdoer" (Rom 13:4).
Where it comes from. From appointment: "whoever resists the authorities resists what God has appointed" (Rom 13:2).

How it co-exists: Fear, and the approval of good conduct: "rulers are not a terror to good conduct, but to bad. Would you have no fear of the one who is in authority? Then do what is good" (13:3); Conscience beside the fear: "Therefore one must be in subjection, not only to avoid God's wrath but also for the sake of conscience" (13:5).
What it leads to. Order: "pay … respect to whom respect is owed" (13:7).
Seat. In the verse: Rom 13:5 "conscience". The subject's own. Genuine. Not read for seat sense in the batches; only the unit-1 side-split lists the verse.

Compared with §37. §37's agents had their own hearts (Assyria, Babylon) and exceeded the commission (also Zec 1:15). §53's agents are appointed. For the person under the authority, the motive to obey is fear of wrath, and beyond it conscience (Rom 13:5).

What it does. "Behold, I will make known to you what shall be at the latter end of the indignation, for it refers to the appointed time of the end" (Dan 8:19). "He shall prosper till the indignation is accomplished; for what is decreed shall be done" (11:36).

How it co-exists: The seer's fear and collapse: "I was frightened and fell on my face … I fell into a deep sleep with my face to the ground. But he touched me and made me stand up" (8:17–18); The proud king prospers within the time: "the king shall do as he wills. He shall exalt himself and magnify himself above every god" (11:36); The wise are refined within it: "some of the wise shall stumble, so that they may be refined, purified, and made white, until the time of the end" (11:35).

What it does. "The princes of Judah have become like those who move the landmark; upon them I will pour out my wrath like water" (Hos 5:10). "Can I forget any longer the treasures of wickedness in the house of the wicked, and the scant measure that is accursed? Shall I acquit the man with wicked scales …?" (Mic 6:10–11).
Where it comes from: Greed: "Your rich men are full of violence; your inhabitants speak lies" (Mic 6:12); Determination: "because he was determined to go after filth" (Hos 5:11).

How it co-exists. What is required instead: "He has told you, O man, what is good; and what does the Lord require of you but to do justice, and to love kindness, and to walk humbly with your God?" (Mic 6:8); "it is sound wisdom to fear your name" (6:9).
What it leads to. Wrath "like water" (Hos 5:10).

Linked to earlier sections. Part A §3 had God's anger on behalf of the widow and orphan (Exo 22:24). Part B §43 had "Execute justice in the morning … lest my wrath go forth" (Jer 21:12). §55 is the same line: injustice among people draws God's anger as surely as idols do.

What it does: "'Yet even now,' declares the Lord, 'return to me with all your heart, with fasting, with weeping, and with mourning; and rend your hearts and not your garments.' Return to the Lord your God, for he is gracious and merciful, slow to anger … Who knows whether he will not turn and relent, and leave a blessing behind him …?" (Joe 2:12–14); The king of Nineveh: "Let neither man nor beast … taste anything … let man and beast be covered with sackcloth, and let them call out mightily to God. Let everyone turn from his evil way and from the violence that is in his hands. Who knows? God may turn and relent and turn from his fierce anger, so that we may not perish" (Jon 3:7–9).

How it co-exists: Fasting and the body, and the heart: "rend your hearts and not your garments" (Joe 2:13). Outward signs are not refused; the heart is named as what must be torn; Awe: "the day of the Lord is great and very awesome; who can endure it?" (Joe 2:11).
What it leads to. "When God saw what they did, how they turned from their evil way, God relented of the disaster" (Jon 3:10). In Jonah the relenting is recorded. In Joel it is left as "Who knows?".
Seat: In the verse: Joe 2:13 "rend your hearts". The hearers' own. Genuine; Outside: Joe 2:12 "with all your heart".

Linked to earlier sections: Part B §43 had "It may be" (Jer 36:7). Part C §39 has "perhaps you may be hidden" (Zep 2:3); Returning that knows no guarantee is a recurring form; Revisit of U1 §13. Jonah's anger at God's mercy (Jon 4) follows this relenting. The mercy he resented was given to a people who turned without knowing it would come.

What it does. "I will bear the indignation of the Lord because I have sinned against him, until he pleads my cause and executes judgment for me. He will bring me out to the light; I shall look upon his vindication" (Mic 7:9).
Where it comes from. From confessed sin, and from trust: "But as for me, I will look to the Lord; I will wait for the God of my salvation; my God will hear me" (7:7).

How it co-exists: Against the enemy's gloating: "Rejoice not over me, O my enemy; when I fall, I shall rise; when I sit in darkness, the Lord will be a light to me" (7:8). The enemy said, "Where is the Lord your God?" (7:10); The one who bears the anger expects God to plead his cause: the same God who is indignant.
What it leads to. Vindication (7:10), then the confession of §5: "Who is a God like you …? He does not retain his anger forever" (7:18).

Compared with earlier sections: Part B §28 asked "correct me, but not in anger". Job and Psalm 88 bore the anger without a cause; Mic 7:9 bears it willingly, with a cause named ("because I have sinned"); Lam 3:39 said the same from another side: "Why should a living man complain … about the punishment of his sins?" (read as context in part B).

What it does. "You brood of vipers! Who warned you to flee from the wrath to come? Bear fruit in keeping with repentance. And do not presume to say to yourselves, 'We have Abraham as our father,' for I tell you, God is able from these stones to raise up children for Abraham" (Mat 3:7–9; Luk 3:7–8).
Where it comes from. From people coming to be baptized: "confessing their sins" (Mat 3:6); in Matthew, "many of the Pharisees and Sadducees" (3:7).
How it co-exists: Urgency: "Even now the axe is laid to the root of the trees" (Luk 3:9); A universal hope: "and all flesh shall see the salvation of God" (Luk 3:6).
What it leads to. Fruit, or the fire (Luk 3:9).
Seat. None in-verse. Outside: Luk 3:6 "all flesh". Humankind.
Linked to earlier sections. Presuming on descent is a form of false peace. "We have Abraham as our father" plays the part of "surely his anger has turned from me" (Jer 2:35).

What it does: "the wrath of God is revealed from heaven against all ungodliness and unrighteousness of men, who by their unrighteousness suppress the truth" (Rom 1:18); "because of your hard and impenitent heart you are storing up wrath for yourself on the day of wrath" (2:5); "for those who are self-seeking and do not obey the truth, but obey unrighteousness, there will be wrath and fury" (2:8); "whoever does not obey the Son shall not see life, but the wrath of God remains on him" (Joh 3:36); "the law brings wrath, but where there is no law there is no transgression" (Rom 4:15).

Where it comes from: Knowledge suppressed: "what can be known about God is plain to them … So they are without excuse" (Rom 1:19–20); Kindness presumed on: "do you presume on the riches of his kindness and forbearance and patience, not knowing that God's kindness is meant to lead you to repentance?" (2:4); Judging others while doing the same: "you who judge those who practice such things and yet do them yourself" (2:3).

How it co-exists: Wrath is paired each time with its opposite:; "eternal life" for "patience in well-doing" (Rom 2:7); "glory and honor and peace for everyone who does good" (2:10); "Whoever believes in the Son has eternal life" (Joh 3:36); "the righteousness of God … from faith for faith" (Rom 1:17); "it depends on faith, in order that the promise may rest on grace" (4:16); Wrath accumulates: "storing up … for yourself" (2:5).
What it leads to. "He will render to each one according to his works" (Rom 2:6).

Seat: In the verse: Rom 2:5 "hard and impenitent heart". The one who presumes, his own. Genuine; Outside:; Rom 2:9 "every human being who does evil" (psyche). Person-sense. Not found in the batches; Joh 3:34 "the Spirit without measure": God's, divine. Not found in the batches.

Linked to earlier sections: Rom 2:5 is part A §21's heart "hardened against turning" and part C's heart "diamond-hard" (Zec 7:12); Rom 2:4 gives the purpose of the delay that §33 described: "God's kindness is meant to lead you to repentance.".

What it does: "we all once lived in the passions of our flesh, carrying out the desires of the flesh and the mind, and were by nature children of wrath, like the rest of mankind. But God, being rich in mercy …" (Eph 2:3–4); "Since, therefore, we have now been justified by his blood, much more shall we be saved by him from the wrath of God" (Rom 5:9); "Jesus who delivers us from the wrath to come" (1Th 1:10); "God has not destined us for wrath, but to obtain salvation" (5:9).
Where it comes from. From God's love shown before any change in them: "while we were still sinners, Christ died for us" (Rom 5:8); "even when we were dead in our trespasses, made us alive" (Eph 2:5).

How it co-exists: A past remembered: "In these you too once walked" (compare Col 3:7); Turning and waiting: "you turned to God from idols to serve the living and true God, and to wait for his Son from heaven" (1Th 1:9–10); Soberness and hope: "let us be sober, having put on the breastplate of faith and love, and for a helmet the hope of salvation" (5:8); Joy: "we also rejoice in God" (Rom 5:11).
What it leads to: Encouragement of others: "Therefore encourage one another and build one another up" (1Th 5:11); Reconciliation: "if while we were enemies we were reconciled to God" (Rom 5:10).

Seat: In the verse: Eph 2:3 "flesh" ×2. The speaker's and the readers' own former way of life. Genuine; Outside: Eph 2:2 "the spirit that is now at work in the sons of disobedience". A hostile spirit.

What it adds: Unit 2 has many who plead against the anger, and some who come through it; Isa 12:1 spoke of the anger as turned away for one person. §60 is the first group that speaks of a wrath still to come as one they are delivered from, while it remains certain for others; The human response is not fear but waiting, soberness and encouragement.

What it does. "What if God, desiring to show his wrath and to make known his power, has endured with much patience vessels of wrath prepared for destruction, in order to make known the riches of his glory for vessels of mercy" (Rom 9:22–23).
Where it comes from. From the human question, which is ruled out: "But who are you, O man, to answer back to God? Will what is molded say to its molder, 'Why have you made me like this?'" (9:20).
How it co-exists: Patience toward the vessels of wrath (9:22); A call that crosses peoples: "even us whom he has called, not from the Jews only but also from the Gentiles" (9:24).

Linked to earlier sections. Isa 64:8 used the same image the other way: "we are the clay, and you are our potter … Be not so terribly angry." In Isaiah the clay pleads with the potter; in Romans the clay is told not to answer back. For the researcher: pointer only.

What it does. "Beloved, never avenge yourselves, but leave it to the wrath of God, for it is written, 'Vengeance is mine, I will repay, says the Lord.' To the contrary, 'if your enemy is hungry, feed him; if he is thirsty, give him something to drink'" (Rom 12:19–20).
How it co-exists: "Repay no one evil for evil" (12:17); "If possible, so far as it depends on you, live peaceably with all" (12:18); "Do not be overcome by evil, but overcome evil with good" (12:21).
What it leads to. Good done to the enemy, and "burning coals on his head" (12:20).

Linked to earlier sections: Part A §24 and part B §24 (the imprecation) asked God to pour out wrath on enemies. Jer 18 showed the intercessor turning to imprecation; Rom 12:19 keeps the same confidence that wrath belongs to God. What changes is the prayer: the wronged person leaves room for the wrath, and feeds the enemy; U1 §31 (the parable master's anger and "forgive your brother from your heart", Mat 18:35) sits beside this. Pointer only.

What it does: "Let no one deceive you with empty words, for because of these things the wrath of God comes upon the sons of disobedience. Therefore do not become partners with them" (Eph 5:6–7); "Put to death therefore what is earthly in you: sexual immorality, impurity, passion, evil desire, and covetousness, which is idolatry. On account of these the wrath of God is coming. In these you too once walked … But now you must put them all away: anger, wrath, malice, slander, and obscene talk" (Col 3:5–8).
Where it comes from. From a former way of life: "at one time you were darkness, but now you are light in the Lord" (Eph 5:8); "Christ who is your life" (Col 3:4).

How it co-exists: Deception about the wrath: "Let no one deceive you with empty words" (Eph 5:6), a New Testament echo of §42; Thanksgiving in place of crude talk: "instead let there be thanksgiving" (5:4).
What it leads to. Walking "as children of light" (Eph 5:8).

Revisit of U1 §25 (VL, "anger in the lists: put off with the old self"). Col 3:8 is in U1 §25. Part C shows that two verses earlier, God's wrath is named as coming on these things (3:6). The human anger to be put off (3:8) stands two verses after the divine wrath that comes (3:6). Revisit note for U1 §25 at consolidation.

What it does: "the great winepress of the wrath of God" (Rev 14:19); "seven angels with seven plagues, which are the last, for with them the wrath of God is finished" (15:1); "seven golden bowls full of the wrath of God" (15:7); "Go and pour out on the earth the seven bowls of the wrath of God" (16:1); "He will tread the winepress of the fury of the wrath of God the Almighty" (19:15).
Where it comes from. From the worship of the beast: "harmful and painful sores came upon the people who bore the mark of the beast and worshiped its image" (16:2).

How it co-exists: The conquerors sing: "those who had conquered the beast … standing beside the sea of glass with harps of God … sing the song of Moses, the servant of God, and the song of the Lamb, saying, 'Great and amazing are your deeds, O Lord God the Almighty! Just and true are your ways'" (15:2–3). Those who have come through confess that the wrath is just; No one can enter: "no one could enter the sanctuary until the seven plagues of the seven angels were finished" (15:8); The struck do not repent: "they cursed the name of God … They did not repent and give him glory".
What it leads to. "It is done!" (16:17); the Word of God on the white horse, "King of kings" (19:13–16).
Seat. None in-verse. Outside: Rev 16:3 "every living thing" (psyche). Life-sense.

Linked to earlier sections: Isa 63:3: "I have trodden the winepress alone." Rev 14:19 and 19:15 take up the winepress. In Isaiah no one helped; in Revelation "the armies of heaven … were following him" (19:14). Pointer only; "The song of Moses" (Rev 15:3). Part A began with the song of the delivered at the sea. Unit 2 ends with the same kind of song, sung by those who conquered.
